A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out. She’s unaware that she’s actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who’s fallen for her, and is certain he’s going to get it right this time.

One day, Rachel, a beautiful young woman, is walking home from work when she’s attacked by a man. The man pulls Rachel into a dark alley, away from the bustling city street. Another man, John, happens to see Rachel getting attacked by the stranger, and decides to help. He grabs the man from behind and shoves him away from Rachel into a pile of garbage bags. The man turns around and looks at John, and then runs away. Rachel is relieved that the man has left her alone, thanks in part to John, who helped her. John and Rachel get to talking, and they realize they have a lot in common. Rachel decides to thank John by going on a date with him to a small, coffee shop the following day. Rachel meets John at the coffee shop and they get to know each other better over cappuccinos. Rachel gets a strange feeling that she knows John very well, but she can't put her finger on it. She dismisses the feeling and they go on a few more dates, and they fall in love. As time goes on, Rachel and John fall deeper in love with each other. They decide to move in together, and they get married. Over the years, Rachel realizes that John has a habit of disappearing for a couple of days. He always comes back, and he always has an excuse.  John tells Rachel that he travels for business at work a lot and he has no choice. Rachel accepts this, but she still has a feeling that something isn’t right. One day, Rachel goes to the store alone and tells John that she will be back shortly. John stays at home and says he has work to do and catch up on. One hour later, Rachel returns from the store and sees John in the backyard acting strange.  Rachel goes to the backyard to see what John is doing, and she sees John digging a hole in the ground. John is burying some shredded clothes, so Rachel asks what he is doing. John tells Rachel that he is burying some old clothes that he doesn’t need anymore. Rachel does not buy John's excuse this time and asks him what is really going on. John tells Rachel that he is a shapeshifter and he has been dating her over and over again. He tells her that he is madly in love with her and has been trying to get it right, so that he could be with her forever. John tells Rachel that she is the only woman he has ever loved, and he will never hurt her again. Rachel is shocked and surprised that John has been doing this for so long. She does not know if she wants to stay with John or leave him. She goes home with her parents and thinks about what John has told her. She realizes that anyone who would go through that much trouble for her is someone worth keeping. Rachel goes back to John and tells him that she loves him and wants to stay with him. John tells Rachel that he will be more honest about his shapeshifting. He tells her that he will tell her when he is going to transform, so she will be prepared. Rachel and John go back in the house and spend the rest of their lives together, happily.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?

In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news? Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world? Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all? Why do you think the way you do?

---

In my opinion, not keeping up with the news does not make you a bad person. Now keeping up with the news does make you slightly better but doesn't mean that you are bad if you don't. I think some people don't want to know what is going on and wants to keep up with their own lives and focus on that. And I don't think that is a bad thing at all. As long as they aren't doing anything harmful then they are a perfectly fine citizen in my book. I think a lot of us anyways see what happens on the news and don't do anything different anyways. Which I feel is the same as not knowing what is happening at all. 

I do think it is good to be informed though. I wouldn't go as far as to say we have a responsibility as citizens to know what is going on but it isn't bad at all to watch the news. Not only would it make you informed but also may make you do something like donate to a group. But in the end, it isn't your responsibility and you shouldn't feel bad if you don't live politically. I would even argue now it is almost better to not like politically or at least make it known about your politics. The topic of politics have been getting bad with Trump losing, vaccines, and wearing masks. And people get a lot of their political information from the news. Some people have a favorite news station that is usually biased to one side of the spectrum. And that doesn't do good as a country to have people rely on one station for all their information.

Overall no not keeping up with the news does not make you a citizen. If you choose to live you life that way then more power to you. I do think it is good though to keep informed. But doing so does not make you a good citizen.

Following World War III, all the nations of the world agreed to 50 years of strict isolation from one another in order to prevent additional conflicts. 50 years later, the United States comes out of exile, only to learn that no one else went into isolation.

America was surprised to learn why.  For some reason, 99% of the rest of the world population had died off. Now all the rest were living in a fallout of sorts caused by nuclear radiation from the nukes of WW3. A world filled with mutants, monsters, and other creatures. The water was poisonous, the air outside was toxic, and crops had a hard time growing. People of the world had banded together in rag tag groups of survivors. Some were just trying to survive, some were trying to rebuild some resemblance of what the world used to be, while other formed bands of bandits roaming around pillaging and stealing whatever supplies they could get from anywhere. 
The world was in a state of chaos.
 America knew it had to really step up and try to help the people of the world. The ones that were surviving and build their own communities. 

So the US started doing missions into the wasteland of the world on rescue missions to bring everyone it could to North America, were land was fertile and water was clean. Best of all, there were no mutants and monsters to fear. They sent ships and planes all around the world. Sent out messages over radio that if people wanted to go, go to the meet up points. People from all over flooded to the meet up points, and went to North America. Slowly over the course of years, people started to rebuild the world to as close to how it used to be. Governments started to reform, and countries started to reestablish themselves.

Once upon a time there was an old mother pig who had one hundred little pigs and not enough food to feed them. So when they were old enough, she sent them out into the world to seek their fortunes. You know the story about the first three little pigs. This is a story about the 92nd little pig.

The 92nd little pig built a house out of depleted uranium. And the wolf was like, "dude."

Choosing depleted uranium wasn't 92's first choice of building material, nor his second, or even his third. But, after realizing that this was a material that none of his other sibling would use, he accepted this as a challenge. 

For generations, Wolf has been the enemy to the pigs and their mother. But after meeting 60 or 70 pigs, Wolf realized he could learn from their determination. Maybe he could even help them from the past mistakes of their elders. He could use his knowledge to meet their needs, and make a mutually beneficial deal. 
The wolf started to teach the pigs how to be shrewd business people. and one of those lessons came in the form of a town who had shut down its nuclear power plant decades ago.

To be fair, the house itself isn't built out of the uranium itself, but the steel containers that hold the product. The wolf and 92nd pig found out that steel containers were either thrown away, buried, or sold for scrap. These were stackable barrels that exuded a faint glow. Pigs being pigs, housekeeping wasn't always the best, yet bugs never entered 92's property.  
Choosing this material also helped 92 make a profit.
 He was provided a recycling reimbursement by the town as long as he agreed to take safety precautions when entering town. Wolf was proud of the accomplishments of his friend 92. The house he advised his friend to build will last forever and the glow of the property will always remind the town of a thrifty little pig named 92.

Your entire life, you've been told you're deathly allergic to bees. You've always had people protecting you from them, be it your mother or a hired hand. Today, one slips through and lands on your shoulder. You hear a tiny voice say "Your Majesty, what are your orders?"

"Finally," you said "What took you so long?"
"This is the first time I've been able to get close enough."
 True your family was extremely overprotective, especially when it came to bees. But you knew the truth. They couldn't stand you and didn't want you around since your brother was more then happy to take over once he came of age. You're not even sure why they kept you around, though having found the secret diary left by your father you had an idea. 

He talked of how you were the true prince and his heir, but he had been ordered to leave you behind and he would never see you again. And how his true identity was King of Bees, but a witch had enchanted him and made him look like a human as punishment. But then he fell in love with a human girl. You were the result of this union, and the queen had taken her anger out on you. The queen, your "mother", who also took human form in order to punish the King for his unfaithfulness.

So you had been waiting, for years, to hear from the bees. And the bee that finally reached you told you the rest of the story. It turned out there were two factions of bees, one loyal to your father and one to the queen. The bees loyal to your father had been trying to get you to safety so that they could release your father from an enchantment, but every time they tried he would lose his memory of you and forget to watch out for you. And so they always failed to reach you.

But today was different. They had gotten word that the queen would be away and you would be alone.Today, they had finally stolen the queen's spell book.Today was the day you became the bee king, and free you father from the spell.
The bee on your shoulder told you to hold out your hand.
 When he landed on it he told you to concentrate on him, and what it would be like to be a bee. And suddenly you were! Now you were truly ready to take back the kingdom.

It was a long drawn out battle, with great feats. near losses, last minute triumph. And at the end, you stood triumphant in front of your father, who was still trapped by the queen's spell. You spoke the words to break the spell, and saw recognition and joy in his eyes. hovered in front of you, and with a cry proclaimed "All Hail the true Bee King!" Your destiny fulfilled, you took over as king and ruled long, and well, and wisely.

For John, he had a fairly uneventful life. He had a fulfilling job, a stable family, and he had plenty of money and time to pursue his hobbies and interests. It would appear that nothing too major would affect him in his life, but that was not the case. For John experienced the oddest event one day, one that would bring about adversity in his life.

His children had gifted him a mug last Father's day, which he cherished and used every day for his morning tea. He liked to drink it to relax before work, and his children were happy whenever they saw him use the mug they bought for him. However, one day they woke up and looked at him funny while he was drinking his tea.
"You get a new mug Dad?" asked his daughter, who was at the time only four years old.
 Puzzled, John replied no. For it was the same mug he drank from every day since last Father's day, a step-up from the plain ceramic mug he used to drink tea from.

Turning the mug around, he noted that his children were indeed correct, the mug he held did not say #1 Dad. In fact it said, #54 Dad. Thinking it was an elaborate prank from his family, John asked his children where his old mug was. They all shrugged their shoulders and said they didn't know. Asking his wife who was heading to work, she seemed as confused as he was regarding the mug, and denied any involvement in the different appearance of the mug.

In any case, John placed the mug in the sink, and would come back to clean it later. He dropped off his kids at school, and returned back home to get to work. Work went on as normal, but when he went to get his mug from the sink he noticed something bizarre. The mug he placed in the sink now said #50 Dad. It dropped down by 4 numbers, he was sure of it. Growing more confused, he thought someone had broken into his house, but he had found no signs of forced entry, and his mug was in the same place he had set it down. Grabbing the mug, he took a picture of it, and made a post online about how odd it was for his mug to say such a thing. Most applauded him for buying such a novel mug, and did not give his incident any further thought.

However, the next day the mug would now say #65 Dad. Like before, John posted the same picture, and people were again amused by the novelty of such a mug. Some even mentioning he had dropped several ranks down, and asked what he did to become worse than he was before.

The following days would be the same type of incidents. He would post the mug with his new rank, which sometimes did not change at all and on other days were fairly different than the day before. He become well known as the man with the changing mug, and people were genuinely interested in the mug, and the reason for it's weirdness. Others were skeptical, and claimed John had multiple mugs made, but his friends and family all supported John, and noted he had quite few mugs stored in his house, with most of them being blank. For the remainder of his life, John had become well known to others not for his notoriety or prestige from his actions or efforts, nor from his job and or position in life. He was known for his novel ceramic mug, which reflected his rank in the world, and showed others that indeed someone or some force was ranking all the dads in the world, and maybe there was a way to measure how good a father a person can really be.

Once upon a time there was an old mother pig who had one hundred little pigs and not enough food to feed them. So when they were old enough, she sent them out into the world to seek their fortunes. You know the story about the first three little pigs. This is a story about the 92nd little pig.

The 92nd little pig built a house out of depleted uranium. And the wolf was like, "dude." And the 92nd little pig was like, "what?" And the wolf was like, "dude, that's not a good idea."

"What do you me," the 92nd pig asked, puzzled.

"That's uranium.  It can kill you," the wolf said.

"How do you know?" the 92nd pig asked.

The wolf explained that he studied chemistry in college.  He started to talk about radioactive elements and the 92nd pig invited him in for tea. "Uhm" the wolf said, "that's not a good idea. I'm not going into your house, and you shouldn't either.  It's too dangerous."

The 92nd little pig looked so pitiful standing there, the wolf introduced himself as Frank and invited him back to his place.  The pig didn't have anywhere else to go, so he packed a bag and followed the wolf.  They went into his den and the wolf turned on the television.  "Sit down," he said to the pig.  Then the wolf went into the kitchen and came back with a tray full of snacks.  "I thought you might be hungry," he said.

The little pig picked up a plate and loaded it with the goodies the wolf had laid out on the tray.  The two of them chatted and watched a football game together in the den.  Finally, as night fell, the 92nd pig asked the question that had been weighing heavily on his all day.  "Frank," he said, "are you going to eat me?"

The wolf looked at him and slowly started to laugh.  He laughed and laughed until tears rolled down his furry cheeks. No," the wolf said, "I'm not going to eat you.
  I'm not going to eat anyone."

"But you're a wolf," the pig said.

The wolf asked the pig what he had eating while they watched tv together.  The pig thought a minute and then said, "let's see, we had peanuts, a fruit salad, a bowl of popcorn and stir fry with tofu for dinner."  

"That's right.  Did you notice that these foods have anything in common?"

he pig thought a minute and then said, "they're all made of plants."


The wolf nodded.

"You're a vegetarian.  You don't eat meat."

"Correct," said the wolf.  "Now, you need a place to stay and I can't pay the rent on this place myself, so how about it.  Do you want to be my roommate?"

The pig agreed, as the place was nice and roomy and not made of depleted uranium like his old place.  He moved in and they lived together happily every after.

A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out. She’s unaware that she’s actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who’s fallen for her, and is certain he’s going to get it right this time.

One day, she meets up with a new guy. This was nothing new, as she loves to meet new people and enjoys to date as many people as she can, hoping that one person will finally be the right fit for her. All of the guys seemed to look good, but they all had the same odd personality quirks. They knew things about her that she did not tell, and she began to feel like they all seemed to actually know her. 

Meeting up with the new guy, John, she is optimistic that things might be different this time around. He is good looking, and seems to be charming. He certainly had a way with words. They were going to her favorite Italian restaurant, and she was running a little behind. When she got to the restaurant, John was already seated waiting for her.

"I'm so sorry I ran late," she exclaimed.

"It's perfectly fine," said John. "I already ordered lasagna for you, your favorite."

Immediately, a few bells of concern rang in her head. "How does he know that my favorite is lasagna?"

She tried to ignore this and turn it into a pleasant date, after all she was already feeling guilty for being late. As the date progressed, John kept seeming to make mention of things that he should not know about her. Just like the past few dates she has been on. She wanted to believe that they were just coincidences, but she was feeling extremely uneasy by now.

As John was getting ready to pay for their meal, she asked "How did you know lasagna was my favorite?"

John said, "Well, I have a confession to make. I actually am John, but I also am Chris, Mike, and Ben. The last three guys you went out with. That's me too."
"I just have fallen so in love with you and I keep blowing it every time we go out. I am a shapeshifter, and so I just change to a different guy and give it another try. You see, I just love you so much I need to make it work one of these times. I know you probably feel uncomfortable, but I promise it is because I love you so much. 

Horrified, the woman ran out of the restaurant. Each of those guys had been creepy and made her feel uncomfortable, and to know that it is just the same guy each time made it much worse for her. She was worried, and she needed to get away from this. She decided that she cannot date anyone for a long time because she will never know if it is this same guy. 

The woman didn't go on any dates for well over a year. In fact, she quit looking for the perfect man altogether.
One day a few years later, she was at the grocery store. She was carrying quite a few products, walking up to the register to pay. She accidentally dropped the bread, and a man behind her picked it up. "Hi, I'm Steve." They began to talk, and Steve asked her to get coffee sometime. She agreed, and the two connected beautifully. After several years, the two got married. They had so much in common.

The one nagging thought she could never get rid of - How did Steve know to ask me for coffee? Coffee was her favorite first date location. How did Steve know that?

Your entire life, you've been told you're deathly allergic to bees. You've always had people protecting you from them, be it your mother or a hired hand. Today, one slips through and lands on your shoulder. You hear a tiny voice say "Your Majesty, what are your orders?"

Now you get why you have been told you were allergic. Because nefarious anti-bee forces wants you powerless, kept from taking your place as the Ruler of the Kingdom of Bees.
But you're not going to let that happen.
 You're going to take your rightful place as ruler of the bees. And you're going to do it by ordering your subjects to do what you want.
You look around, and see a hive.
 You walk over to it and give a command in a whisper. The hive responds, and you hear a buzzing sound. You repeat this process a few times, and instruct your subjects to spread your orders far and wide.
You've also just created a distributed system that is a lot like a blockchain.

The blockchain is a distributed ledger.
 It's a way of storing information that is shared across a network of computers. This ledger is updated by a consensus mechanism, so that everyone on the bee network knows the current state of the ledger.

The next day, many bees stream out of the air vents in a data center in Belarus. They fly around the datacenter, and land on the servers. When a technician approaches, they stream through his ears and into his brain, where they take command of the person's neural network.
The technician walks over to a rack of servers and gtypes  command.


Far away, you stare at a computer screen which updates your Bitcoin balance. It goes from zero to five thousand, then ten, then a hundred. Soon you've made a billion dollars. Or the bees have made it for you, by using their distributed system to make an addendum to the Belarus' servers blockchain with their own Bee-Blockchain. The next morning Bitcoins are renamed "Beecoin", puzzling techies, who grudgingly accept the change as the probable work of the Winklevoss twins.
The bees have just created a new cryptocurrency.

This is the future of blockchain.


You smile as you raise a spoonful of honey to your lips.

When you're 28, science discovers a drug that stops all effects of aging, creating immortality. Your government decides to give the drug to all citizens under 26, but you and the rest of the “Lost Generations" are deemed too high-risk. When you're 85, the side effects are finally discovered.
The Lost Generations is a story about the lives of the people who were denied immortality, and how they cope with their lives.

A specific part of the population was chosen to receive immortality and those above the age of 26 are denied that immortality. The story is told through the eyes of a man who is 28 and is part of the Lost Generations. This man who we will call William, has been happy with the result of not receiving immortality. William has watched others experience the side effects of having immortality and he is glad that he is not a part of this experiment. William is a man who is happy with his life and is content with the decision not to receive immortality. William has seen severe side effects in those who have taken the drug. The side effects have included such tiredness that people cannot function and just want to sleep as a result. Many people have experienced an appetite that cannot be satiated so they are never content with any amount of food that they consume. This is one of the more severe side effects that leaves people constantly hungry, never full and never satisfied. William has seen people who have taken the drug and have gone insane and have committed suicide. Severe obesity has been a very serious medical complication as a result of constant and unending hunger.  Another unwanted side effect is that people have become unable to move because of the obesity and their size. William has found in his interactions, that those who took the immortality drug are regretful and wish that they never took it. Unfortunately there is no resolve to this dilemna for these people since it is now too late. William remains happy and content with his natural life cycle and is grateful for the time that he does have and uses it to his full advantage.

Lana has been dating ever since she graduated high school, but it never works out in the end for her. The guys she dates seem interesting and are fun to be around, however there always seems to be some distance between them despite her attempts to get closer to her dates. The truth of the matter is that she is unaware that she's actually been dating the same guy over and over since high school, that is she has been the crush of a shapeshifter for the past couple of years.
After she breaks up with the latest guy she's been dating, she finds herself attracted to her new neighbor, Alex.
 Alex had recently moved in from New York, and had done so after his company has moved to her state. He works in marketing, as a visual designer. They seem to share common interests, but Lana is less interested in that given that the past men she has date all shared her interests as well. One day, Alex asks if he can take Lana out to dinner. Lana accepts, seeing it as an opportunity for her to get close to Alex and learn more about him. 

Going on a date with Alex to a new restaurant, Lana finds the experience interesting, yet at the same time, strangely familiar. Alex seems to hit it well with her, being into the things she likes, such as shows, movies, and even food. However, whenever she presses him on certain questions, she finds that he seems to change the subject, or come up with a reason why he can't talk about it. She doesn't hear about him about many topics about his past, such as where he went to school, his family, or even what he was like as a child. Alex always seems to prefer talking about Lana and his current interests than divulging information about his past. It doesn't come too much as a surprise to Lana, as it seems that is a recurring theme for her past dates and boyfriends, and she tries to enjoy the rest of the evening. They eventually head on back, with Alex wishing her well as he heads back into his apartment. 

As she goes back into the apartment, she ponders whether to continue dating Alex or not. She then hears strange noises, and learns it is coming from Alex's apartment. Worried, she heads out and knocks on his door, noticing it is unlocked. She heads inside, and discovers that bitter truth about Alex. Seeing him changing into someone else, Lana confronts Alex about what she saw. Alex reveals that he is a shapeshifter, and that he has been dating her for the past couple of years. Lana is confused and shocked, which later turns to a strong sense of betrayal as Alex has deceived her all these past years. He tries to explain why he has been dating her, which he claims is because he feels she is his soul mate. Lana understands, but tells Alex why she overall broke up with him in the past. Realizing his secrecy is the root cause for their break-ups, he then promises Lana to be more open to her in the future, and that he is willing to stop hiding who he truly is. Lana after some time pondering, accepts Alex's apology and they both go on to start their relationship anew. While it would take some time for her to trust in her odd neighbor, she is secretly delighted. For once, the person she is dating is completely honest with her, and she feels closer to him than anyone else she had dated in the past, even if it was the same person in different forms.

When you die, you appear in a cinema with a number of other people who look like you. You find out that they are your previous reincarnations, and soon you all begin watching your next life on the big screen.

"This can't be happening to me", I thought to myself.  "Am I still alive?  Is this all one big dream?  The last thing that I remember is going to bed next to my wife".  Someone who looked like an 18 -year old version of me walked up to where I was sitting.   He told me that he knew how it felt when he first got here.  He was scared.  "You get used to it, though", he said.    "How long have you been here?", I asked.  "FDR was president when I died", he replied.

"Wow.  So, we just sit here and watch how our future selves live their life?", I whispered to him.   "Yep.  This is an endless cycle.  I am not sure what will happen when more of us get into the cinema.  There are only so many seats in here.  Maybe, we will get a nice theater upgrade down the road", he said.

 sat there thinking about the life I just left behind.
  I started to feel claustrophobic.  I needed to get out of the theater.  I asked my younger version if anyone has tried to leave the theater before.  "Actually, no.  Not since I have been here", he said.  
I got up, walked toward the exit of the theater, and discovered that there was no door.
  There was an exit sign, but the "door" was painted on the wall.  I looked back at my younger self, and then at the other people sitting in the theater.   "I guess I am going to be here for a while.  I may as well get comfortable", I thought to myself.

I went back to sit in my seat.  I took a deep breath in and started watching the adventures my reincarnated self.  I hope they don't make the same mistakes that I did.

A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out. She’s unaware that she’s actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who’s fallen for her, and is certain he’s going to get it right this time.

One day, the woman and the shapeshifter have date at swanky wine bistro in the trendy part of town. For this "first date" the shapeshifter has come as Dirk Haynes, a wealthy man about town.
The woman is late, and when she arrives, she’s in a hurry.
 She seems to barely pay attention to any of Dirk's well-chosen lines. She’s distracted, and she’s late for something.

Finally Dirk can't help but ask: "Am I keeping you from something?"
"No, but I’m late for something," she says.


"What are you late for?" asks Dirk.
"I’m late for my date with you," she says.


This flummoxed Dirk. "But you are not late, you're here," he said.
"Yes, but I'm late for my date with you," she said.


Dirk had an idea. "Just who do you think I am?" he asked her.
"You're Dirk Haynes," she said.
 "But you remind me of the last guy I dated" she continued. "He was a little bit like you, but he was a little bit different."

"How so?" Dirk asked.
""He wasn't such a putz," opined the woman.
Dirk was taken aback.
 "But that was me," he said.
"No, you're Dirk Haynes," she said.


"Sure I'm Dirk." said the man. "But I was also Matt Cuchosz, Steve Arnott, and even Captain Hastings, the last three guys you dated."
"No," she said.
 "And besides, aren't the last two characters from 'Line Of Duty'?"
"NIs the show on now? I think it is" said Dirk.


"Do you want to come over and watch it?" asked the woman.

"Sure'" he said. "This could be the start of a beautiful friendship!"
"I'm not sure," she said.
 

But do you know what?

It was.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?

Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous. Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not? Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?

---

In my opinion, it is not selfish to engage in extreme sports, so long as the risk is only to one's self.   What is selfish is to inflict the risk on someone else, like your family, friends or even innocent bystanders.  However, this is extremely rare in the case of what I generally think of as "extreme sports", and is perhaps much more common in more traditional team sports or, especially, in auto racing.  

There is, of course, the question of whether or not this risk is acceptable, even in rare cases, but I would argue that spectators at auto races, and especially those who crowd around the dirt tracks at rally events, knowingly and willingly take on that risk.
IBack to the question at hand,  believe much of the danger is a result of what participants want from extreme sports.
  Most of what I think of as extreme sports are a contest in which an individual pushes his or her own personal limits.  This could be on a skateboard in a stunt park, or on the side of a remote mountain.  In these cases, they are really only risking their own life and limb, and as long as they are prepared to pay the consequences, they should be allowed to do so.  
However, it becomes selfish to the point of being dangerous when such risk forces others, who might not know better or be aware of the risks
 to pay some of the ultimate cost.  If an extreme athlete is uninsured, or has publicly provided health insurance, he or she is passing on the cost of any potential injury to the broader community.  You could make the case that even a fully-insured athlete is using hospital resources that might be better applied elsewhere, but I feel that this is not really salient.  If one were to take this position, we would have to consider children selfish every time they take a risk, and I am not willing to go that far.  It is the willful refusal (or inability) to pay for the consequences of one's actions that I consider to be selfish, and most extreme athletes do not engage in such conduct.  
However, I am not willing to completely dismiss the notion that some sports are too dangerous to be considered sporting events at all.
  One on one combat is a genre of sports that definitely comes close to, and sometimes crosses this line.  I would agree that athletes should be allowed to engage in boxing, wrestling, or other martial-arts contests that involve physical contact and serious risk of injury to themselves and to their counterpart, but only if they are fully aware of what they are doing.  Obviously, those under 18 or those who are not otherwise considered mentally-able to sign a contract should be barred from these sports for that reason.  And, of course, if someone chose to engage in combat sports without adequate ability to pay for potential injuries, I would consider that action to be selfish.  They are unduly burdening others in society for the sake of their own excitement.

So, ys, there are risks when engaging in extreme sports, but it is important to remember that there are risks in most sports. and in most aspects of daily life.  I hope that my point has been clear, that others should be free to take these risks with their own bodies, and with the bodies of willing co-participants.  

What would be selfish, would be forcing the risk of any kind of harm, including financial harm, on others who do not consent. 

The true question, and the one that should be addressed in public policy, is how to stop this behavior from propagating among those who may not.  Should a group insurance pool be set up for extreme athletes?  This is a practical question that could benefit from further discussion, but for now, I think my point has been clear, and I thank you for reading.

In my opinion, having a period is definitely a naturally occurring bodily function that is not shameful. Firstly, how our government should allocate budget with getting rid of period poverty. Instead of allocating more funds in our military or in the police force, our government should allocate more funds in providing free pads and tampons to students. Senators are granted budgets for their Viagra pills and other medications, but why are our schools do not get budgets for free pads and tampons? This is daylight robbery, and our students in this country has had enough.

Second, proper history, education, and awareness of periods should be taught in schools. How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, it's a two way street when it comes to our screened devices. In one way, we can argue that the screens we have everyday make our lives easier, more entertaining, and more productive. On the other hand, too much screen usage makes our social interactions more limited and less meaningful. So it is a delicate balance of how much is too much of the ever evolving digital world, and there isn't yet a standard for how much screen time is healthy.

In recent news, China has banned children under the age of 18 from playing online games. Is this cruel and unfair? Definitely. But is this because of an over-abundance of screen time causing the addiction and consequently the behavioral issues that we see in our youth today? It's also a possibility. That's why it's always a two-fold and multi-faceted discussion when it comes to something that can become exponentially more influential, powerful and persuasive with time.

What I suggest is that parents, companies, and the government should step in and try to change the nature of our screen habits, before this new digital world starts overtaking the more traditional ways of life of our evolution. The company, Facebook, has started removing the notifications feature on their home screen because of all the incessant distracting "Likes" and "+1's". Google has also implemented the "Do Not Disturb" feature to help you turn off your phone at night, if that's what you want to do. However, these steps are just the initial steps and the companies need to do more to ensure that we aren't getting lost in our digital world.

China's banning of people under the age of 18 from playing games is an extreme and drastic step to take, and I wouldn't want to see this type of action taken in the United States. Instead, a federal law to urge app makers and companies to monitor the screen habits of our youth might be more effective in preventing things like compulsive gambling, compulsive shopping, compulsive texting, and any type of addiction that leads to more unnecessary screen time.

Educators and parents should also step up to ensure our kids are not losing valuable time in their development, health, and social life because they are lost within the confines of their screens. A more hands-on approach and a more sensitive level of mentorship for our youth can reduce the let-down from our digital world by introducing more hands-on experiences and personality. If you are a parent, spending more time and having activities with your kid would help them spend less time on their phones.

To recap, I never want any banning or any drastic measures for people to limit their screen time. It doesn't work and it will not deter people from not using their devices. Instead, we should talk about the nuanced, more specific and technical aspects about how to balance the modern lifestyle with the ways of our ancestors. This can be done by analyzing and studying different aspects of life like our social interaction, our health, and our cognitive ability, where all of these three aspects are intertwined. Having devices with screens will not go anytime soon, but I just hope for the sake of our survival, devices will play a more positive role in our daily routines instead of the other way around.

---

In my opinion, there are many benefits to audiobooks. Many people are on the go with limited free time. Audiobooks enable people to listen to books while working on other projects. Also, audiobooks can be especially good for students and children, who can listen on the way to/from school or while playing outside. Furthermore, some people seem to learn better via audio over sight. Listening to books can be a great way to work through reading tasks and gain a new perspective on what one has read.

However, there is something lost when listening to audiobooks. Books can be transportive, making it hard to truly immerse oneself in a book when listening instead of reading. There is a sense of progress and oneness while reading a physical book that is a bit lost when you can't literally feel the number of pages thinning as you race towards the end. There are many small lessons a book reader innately absorbs about language arts, too. Book readers--via exposure--are almost certainly better spellers, with an elevated sense of what's possible with vocabulary, sentence structure, and when to use different punctuation marks. A person also has to simultaneously conceptualize the scene in their mind and picture it in their head while reading. People do this to some extent with audiobooks, but the audio will play on even while the listener has mentally begun to daydream. Book readers have a natural advantage here, too, where if their mind begins to drift, they simply cease progressing through the story, and can pick right back up where they left off. 


So, audiobooks are not for everybody.
 It largely depends on what each person wants to get out of the book.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, there is a real risk. Just because society has shifted its focus to a more pressing issue, doesn't mean that we don't still have a screen time problem. 
The real problem isn't the time that kids spend on their smart phones, tablets or computer screens.
 The problem is what they do with that time. We've watched them, through the pandemic, learn from virtual classrooms. This is an example of good screen time. We have also seen many children submerge into online gaming to an unhealthy level, as well as some other social networking applications that have created a diversion that leads to an unhealthy amount of time on a screen. 
We saw with this pandemic and the way society responded that most parents did not have a sufficient amount of control over how their children could use
 their devices. It is common today for kids to have access to their own screen, and many of them have built a simulated life on the networks. These networks have digital stores, simulated cities that are part of multiplayer games, and have access to an online news station that keeps kids up with current events. There is a lot of good there but, as with anything else, there can be such a thing as too much of a good thing. 
It's time to begin talking about the opposite of screen time, which is life time.
 Too many kids have been living through the pandemic in isolation. They haven't had the opportunity to go out and build new, real world, relationships. That has led to a lot more screen time than ever before. The more that kids use their screen devices, the less time they have for human contact and interaction in the real world. Since many of them have been stuck at home, if they don't get that interaction from immediate family they find that they can get it online. 

Unfortunately, the need for physical interaction pressures anyone that doesn't have a lot of friends to begin craving more and more screen time. It's an addiction, and it should be treated as such. We don't encourage addicts to continue to use. We shouldn't encourage kids using their devices for 18 hours of a 24 hour day to continue staring at the screen. Humans have a natural need for human contact and all of us, kids and adults, need the real world interaction even-more during stressful times like this

I believe that the best thing we can do for our kids is to give them the interaction that they crave. It can be difficult to find the energy to do that, after working all day, but it's more than worth the effort. 
The real world is where life occurs.
 We need to get our kids back into the real world. The screen world can be a really fun place, and there's a lot to learn, but it's not so very different than any other addiction. We need to offer an alternative and the best way to do that is to interact with them ourselves. I encourage everyone who reads this article to spend some time with their kids today. No phones and no computers allowed.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?

Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous. Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not? Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?

---

What is a sport? Is it a personal quest for achievement?

Hardly.

A sport is a business, and its purpose is to make money, pure and simple. A sport gets played because it makes money for the owners and players. Nowhere in the calculation of profit does it consider the risk to the participants. As long as the public will buy tickets, watch on TV, buy sports apparel, cheer them on as heroes and call their names from the stands, anything goes. he owners do not care whether their employees are alive or dead, so long as they make money.


The idea that society owes a duty of protection to athletes who are budding millionaires, and choose their sport voluntarily, is quaint. Although some may expect them to avoid activities that may result in their premature death, it is not our duty. Capitalism is amoral, money talks, and ethics fall by the wayside.
When we see a wealthy 23-year -ld pextreme slorts payer being carried on an air stretcher after rupturing a disk in his back,
 we shrug and wait for the next match. If the player is cured, you can bet they will be right back in the arena. And if he is forced into retirement, then just wait for the movie and book deals.

rensome sports too dangerous to play?
 By what standards could this be even determined? The players are earning a living, and they may be willing to risk their lives, for better or worse. And the point of sports is to push limits and boundaries. 

Without risk, there is no sport. As long as there is a demand for high-risk athletes, there will be someone willing to take the chances. And that demand shows no sign of abating. So long as profits exceed the risks, the high-risk sports will persist.

And we should remember that hardly anything is safe anyway.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?

Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous. Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not? Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?

---

In my opinion, extreme sport are not to dangerous to be sports. Of course there needs to be some restrictions on them - mountains should be closed of the conditions are dangerous, same with surfing areas, skateparks should be inspected for structural safety, etc. But it is a personal risk which one chooses to do, and that personal choice should remain once all reasonable precautions have been taken.
But generally, sports are about testing yourself.
 All sports can result in terrible injury; think about all the recent controversies recently around concussions especially in football and soccer. And all of the terrible, literally bone shattering, injuries that happen in gymnastics. And yet we allow it, or at least don't prevent it - why? Because those sports are traditional ones, and we have long since become accustomed to the dangers of them. But most extreme sports are new, and from the comparison, seem more dangerous. 

Some people might say that the cost of these sports is passed on to others, including people with no interest in the sport. For example a rescue mission to retrieve stranded mountain climbers can costs thousands and thousands of dollar of public service and rescue worker funds, and can be dangerous for the rescue workers as well.  But the same is true in the case of a terrible traffic accident, or a construction incident, fishing boats caught in storms etc. And those are far more common, as far more people choose to drive, or work dangerous jobs. But those things are considered necessary, and so the risk is ignored. 

Finally, while extreme sports are risky, like with any activity they will become less risky over time. As more is learned about them, and more safety measures are developed, the dangers will decrease. And it would be sad to lose such exciting and enjoyable activities due to fear. 

So I say those who want to participate in extreme sports should be allowed to do so freely, as long as they understand the risks.

Should Schools Provide Free Pads and Tampons?

Have you ever experienced period shaming, or “period poverty"? Should schools step in to help? Should schools be required to provide free pads and tampons to students? How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools? How are they different?

---

While I have not ever experienced period shaming or period poverty, I know that such incidents exist from the perspectives of my close friends and the people I have interacted with in my life. I can emphasize nonetheless with their stigmas, and feel that such incidents should be prevented for females students for what is effectively a natural and widespread human experience. To prevent such stigmas and negative social demeaning,schools should provide free pads and tampons to students.
 Such items are relevant to the interests of schools as institutions of learning, and are necessary for the health and well-being of students that cannot easily afford such items. In addition, many students should view schools as safe environments for them to learn and interact with fellow students, for often they might lack such comfort at home or elsewhere in their life. By roviding free pads and tampons to students., they can ensure that female students can feel supported during a stressful time in their life, that they are unfamiliar with at times and potentially do not have the financial means to afford the items that alleviate the symptoms of periods. 
Pads and tampons are similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools.
 For the most part, pads and tampons do not need to be inherently viewed as negative or dangerous. Pads and tampons intend to stop bleeding from staining clothes, similar to how Band-Aids do for other parts of the body. They are essentially hygienic items, and should be viewed as such to the same degree people view toilet paper, soap, and other items that are used frequently to maintain hygiene. The main difference between pads and tampons relate to the fact that they are used for a more private and personal purpose, and are not as readily available in stores. In a school setting, pads and tampons ought to be distributed in a discreet manner, not disclosing the female students identity when they request for them, nor telling the other students that said student needs free pads or tampons. Unlike the usage of toilet paper, Band-Aids, and soap, tampons and pads as mentioned can be a source of ridicule and bullying for the students. Despite the widespread use of pads and tampons, there are still many people who view them as taboo or dirty, especially male students that are in middle or high school. In any case, schools should still provide pads and tampons based on the benefits they bring to female students that require them and cannot access them by personal finances or means. Schools should take great efforts to avoid incurring stigmatization towards female students that request such products, by maintaining their confidentiality and privacy when asking and receiving the products.

Schools should take a more active role in reducing and stopping the incidence of period shaming and period poverty. Their experiences have been very impactful to my thoughts and perspectives, and I empathize with the pain and discomfort they have gone through in school. These items should not be viewed as costs to the schools, but rather investments in ensuring the health and well-being of its students, who often have a hard time just talking about bodily functions due to societal taboos. Ensuring the health and well-being of its students will be of great benefit to their education, as, without both, one can not function optimally nor focus on their studies and learning.

Pads and tampons are quite similar to other hygienic items, especially bandages and plasters offered by the school. Privacy must be maintained for the female students, as it ensures their comfort and ease in asking for said items. Furthermore, schools should ensure that the female students’ access to such items are as easy as possible, as those with periods may already suffer from pain and would not want to go through difficult means to acquire them. Pads and tampons ought to be available in schools freely for students that require them, as they are beneficial to their comfort and education, but care must be taken to ensure that their distribution does not cause further ridicule or shaming from the other students.

Humans once wielded formidable magical power. But with over 7 billion of us on the planet now, Mana has spread far too thinly to have any effect. When hostile aliens reduce humanity to a mere fraction, the survivors discover an old power has begun to reawaken once again.
The story begins with a young man named Riku, who lives in a world where magic has long been forgotten.
 He has been raised in Landro by his grandfather Frezna, a wizard, and has always dreamed of becoming a great wizard himself.  Riku didn't know what had ever happened to his parents; his grandfather refused to tell him.  He lived a lonely, isolated life and longed for a family outside his grandfather.  There were no photographs of his parents; the only picture was of a woman.  Sometimes he would see his grandfather gazing at the photograph, a wistful look on his face.  

His grandfather spent years training him, but it takes a long, long time to learn everything one needs to know to use magic to its full extent.  When Riku was 14, his grandfather passed away.  Riku had been kept at home his whole life and knew little about the world, but now he had to set out and find his way.  He decided to go to the city of Faltra, where he had heard from his grandfather that there were many people who could teach him about magic.
Riku's first day in Faltra is a disaster.
  They spoke a different dialect than he had learned growing up, so it was very difficult to get around.  He did have a little money and was finally able to find a room to rent.  He knew he needed to find a job, and find someone to continue teaching him magic.  Over the next few weeks, he learned the dialect and started to find his way around the city.  He got a job at a bakery, where he worked hard and met a lot of people as he waited on them.  He made friends with a young girl named Selphie, who was a waitress at the bakery.  They became friends immediately, and it was almost like they had known one another forever.

One day, Selphie invited Riku to come to her house for dinner.  Selphie lived with her grandmother. He arrived with some flowers he had picked.  When he knocked on the door, an elderly woman opened it.  Riku stood in the doorway, frozen solid.  It was an older version of the woman in the photograph that his grandfather had.  Riku knew it had to be her; he too had spent hours looking at that photograph.  The woman also stood very still, staring at him.

"Riku," she said.  "Is it you?"

"Have we met?" Riku asked?

"Have you come here from Landro?"

"Yes," Riku said.

"Is Frezna your grandfather,"

"Yes," Riku responded.

"Where is he?"

"He died, and I came to Faltra to find someone to continue my magic education."

The woman motioned him inside, and sat heavily on the sofa, tears running down her face.  She told Riku she was his grandmother, and when his parent were killed by magic hunters, she and her husband had each taken one of the children and fled to keep them safe and keep teaching them magic.  Selphie was his sister!  By this point, she had joined them in the parlor and they both listed to the story their grandmother told.  She was teaching Selphie magic, but neither Riku nor Selphie's magic would be strong until they were reunited, as they were twins.  She hadn't known that her husband had passed away.  They hadn't seen each other in nearly 12 years, but had kept in touch as best they could.  

Riku and Selphie were overjoyed to be reunited, and they spent the evening talking and catching up. Riku and Selphie spent the next year honing their magic and making plans for how to use their powers to return Mana to its past glory.  That would be their next adventure.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?

In my opinion, people are more empathetic to an animal suffering because people feel that animals are like kids in a way. Animals are not really capable of fending for themselves or living on their own the majority of the time. So when an animal is suffering or beaten, it sort of is similar to a little baby being beaten. I think in a way, if were to be so upset about it each and every time we would drive ourselves crazy mentally. Its the same feeling you would get if you saw a infant that was left outside by itself, or if you saw someone harming a little baby. The baby can not protect itself, so your instinct is to go and help it. 

I personally dont feel it is wrong to focus on animal suffering, as i feel that if you are focused on helping anyone that is suffering it is a good deed. As far as where to dictate our funds as a country, i think it would be smarter to help people out. Helping people out would be an investment anyway, and this would allow those people who were helped to help out the animals. The more healthy people we have, the more homes we have for these animals. The best thing we can do i would say would be to treat these animals right and give them great lives while they are here. So in conclusion, i dont think it is WRONG to focus on animal welfare, however i feel that human suffering is a larger problem.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?

Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten? Or that other researchers found that if forced to choose, 40 percent of people would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist.

Why do you think many people are more empathetic toward the suffering of animals than that of people? In your opinion, is it wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering? Why do you think so?

---

In my opinion, I think that people tend to be more concerned about individual cases, whether human or animal, more so than statistics, so I am not surprised to hear that research subjects were more upset about the idea of a dog being beaten than the idea of a human being similarly beaten.  It is a simple fact that people are somewhat inured to violence against humans because we see so much of it in the media, and yet violence against charismatic animals such as dogs or seals is both shocking and upsetting to us.  

We have to remember that this result came from a laboratory.  If people were in a real situation in which they could either stop an unfamiliar dog from being beaten, or a stranger from being beaten, I doubt that anyone would choose the dog.
I tdo not hink that iitwis rong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering, bsimply because the former grabs our attention more acutely.  Bt I do think that we need to be careful not
 make decisions that have real-world consequences using only our feelings, rather than our rational thoughts.  For example, we might oppose the hunting of whales, yet if a small community of indigenous people are only able to survive through the winter by sustainably killing one whale per year for meat and blubber, then we should not let our idealistic view of noble, graceful animals distract from the needs of real, living persons.  

As for the other question of people preferring to save their own dog, rather than the life of a foreign tourist, I cannot really judge anyone too harshly.  How many of us could truly say that we would prefer to save a stranger over a family member?  Wouldn't you prefer to save your estranged uncle even if it meant allowing two or more other people to die as a result?  People are close to their pets, and treat them as family, so it is not surprising, or unethical, for us to prioritize their welfare.  My main objection is treating the vague idea of an animal as more valuable than the real-world welfare of a human.  

This, of course, leads to more philosophical questions, and ones that I cannot give a confident answer to.  For example, is it wrong to eat meat?  Humans benefit from the nutritional density of meat, but animals are obviously harmed.  I think that this is a personal choice that each individual should make, and one that they shouldn't make lightly.  As long as they are aware of the fact that animals suffer for their convenience, then (with some serious regulations in place to prevent extreme suffering) they should be allowed to do so.  Likewise, I tend to favor animal research for medical purposes, because ultimately, a lot more suffering is prevented than is caused.  But, of course, I accept that this is not always a utilitarian calculation.  Some may feel that it is wrong to deliberately harm an animal or a human, and I respect that opinion.

In so many words, I can understand why people tend to favor the lives of highly-visible animals over the lives of unseen humans, but I do have to strenuously object.  The needs of the many, as it were, far outweigh the needs of the few.

---

In my opinion, dating apps dramatically improve the dating experience. I have used several of them, to varying degrees of success. My measure of success is whether or not I had an enjoyable experience, and more often than not, I have. 
I think dating apps are great because they allow you to meet people who you would not normally meet.
 In a typical day, I don't get much opportunity to meet new people. Time is usually accounted for, and I don't have enough free time to spend at typical hook up spots. Dating apps allow me to meet people who I would not otherwise meet, and it's a great way to get out of my comfort zone.

Technology makes dating better, outside of the dating app world as well. Apps like Netflix and having the freedom to text rather than a voice call help to keep the pressure fairly low and give me the opportunity to keep the lines of communication open. I've done virtual dates using Netflix, where we both queued up a movie at the same time, at remote locations. It was a lot of fun. 
I think technology has the potential to make dating better, but it also has the potential to make it worse.
 It can be hard to judge if there will be chemistry between two people until they have met, in person. I've had a few uncomfortable experiences, where the date was just not enjoyable for either of us. We just didn't click. I think that's a risk you take with any dating experience, but I think it's a risk worth taking.

I think that a lot of people have already used dating apps. I'm quite sure that a lot more people will utilize them in the future. They are convenient, exciting and efficient. Even when dates don't work out, the experience is still an adventure. Even if it doesn't blossom into a romantic encounter, meeting new people is usually a growth experience. Dating apps facilitate that. One thing for sure is, whether you love them or hate them, dating apps are here to stay.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?

Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous. Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not? Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?

---

In my opinion, a person is ultimately the one that dictates the level of risk and or safety they can undertake in their life. What they decide to do with their life, is primarily their decision. Risky sports such as extreme mountain climbing, is an active decision that people take, just like other athletes that perform less risky sports. Extreme sports are not for everyone, but for those that do choose to participate, it is their choice to do so. They are not forced to do so, nor are the dangers hidden from them when they being investing time in the sport. Less dangerous sports will always draw more people to it, primarily for the ease in getting proficient in said sports, but also the fact that such sports will not injure them if precautions are taken. The same can be applied to extreme sports, as mountain climbing can be done in a risky manner, or in a way that minimizes dangers and reduces the risk for the person. 

Whether a sport is then too dangerous does not change its classification, as sports are labeled not based on the risk involved in the sport, but rather how the person engages in it, and whether they compete or even cooperate with others. Extreme sports follow the same set of guidelines as many less risky sports, but are associated with more risk. For example, people wishing to mountain climb must learn proper techniques, invest in proper equipment, and even train on less tasking mountains before tackling more dangerous and demanding climbs. The same is true for other extreme sports. 

As for when a sport becomes unreasonable or still within reason depends primarily on the person, specifically their skill, physique, and mindset. For example, a person who is not in good physical shape, or does not have the proper mindset to climb a mountain, will be more likely to get injured on the climb than a more experienced climber. Thus we could say for the person that it is unreasonable for them to continue to mountain climb, until they get more experience and training. There might as well be some level that is unobtainable for athletes and participants of an extreme sport, that might be considered based on risk and danger to be unreasonable to undertake no matter the physique and training said participants may have. Ideally, they ought to be well informed of the risks and dangers, and well-prepared for the sport. To disregard such considerations is to make the sport more risky than it already is, but many do make such considerations. n the end, it is up to the person to decide what they are willing to risk in their life., and what sort of achievements they wish to accomplish, either for the notoriety or for some sense of self-worth.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?

Do you think college athletes should be paid? Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In “Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports," Cody J. McDavis writes: “Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games). But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni. A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford."

Do you find his argument persuasive? What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?

---

In my opinion, there are many pros and cons to paying college athletes. I personally feel that it is less problematic to not pay college athletes and for this reason i would side with not paying them. However, i think the root of the problem just comes with the large amount of money schools make off of these college athletes. NCAA is one of the highest payed organizations in the world, and much of this is because they dont have to pay their athletes. This makes people refer to the athletes almost like they are being taken advantage of. I understand the perspective of the athlete being taken advantage of, however they are still given the platform to demonstrate their skills, and also given the opportunity to play in front of large crowds and meet tons of people, and build a following on social media. Many perks come with being a college athlete aside from just possibly being paid. The free tuition is nice for the athlete, however i dont know how much paying the athletes would be helpful. Would they be paid based off of talent, or just a flat fee? If it was a flat fee, the athletes would probably want more anyway if they were the star players. I am personally a former college football player as well, and I just feel that it is not necessary to pay the players. I think it would be nice to have more in place for the athletes, but not necessarily just a pay check. I know there are some athletes who can barely afford college and food while being there. This is unexceptable to me if they are part of a team making that much money for the university. I would treat it like a job and simply provide the best working conditions for athletes that do a lot to help the school run. No student athlete at all should have to worry about getting food to eat, or having a place to stay. I think this is a good compromise to the problem. Using some of the money to give back to athletes instead of giving athletes the freedom to spend on whatever they wish. 

I am for the side of not paying athletes because i think there are too many variables associated with the amount you would pay them, and it is also sort of starting a bidding process right out of high school. College would almost be like the pros in a way if you could get paid like a professional athlete. If anything i think a flat fee would be most fair for everyone who was a part of the actual team. This way, nobody is glorified in the amount that they are paid. This would literally create powerhouses and the same schools would win every year just because they have the most money. I think it would be a good idea to have a stipend for the athletes as well, just to make sure that they are able to make ends meet. Just more structured types of payment that is more equal to all of the players on the team. There are simply too many downsides of paying each player based off of their value, and i dont think it would be something that would be easy to bounce back from for the NCAA. All this being said, the NCAA has to stop being stingy with their money and simply treat the athletes better. If this was the case, this would not even be a discussion. In conclusion however, i feel that the NCAA should not pay college athletes, at least in the same way pro players are paid.

 Son? As in he is claiming to be your father? Your mother never mentioned your father, or rather, she said he was a short, foreign romance and the man had left in the night to go back to his home and that was it.

When reading, a person can set their own pace and decide for themselves how long to spend with the book, not having to worry about listening time. In addition, they can become more invested in the literature, as reading makes the person more able to picture the events of the story, and even gives the reader greater input in how the story is read, as audiobooks have set narrators that voice the characters and events of the story. For me, these are appealing benefits that draws me more to reading, than to listening to an audiobook. That isn't to say as mentioned I would discourage the use of audiobooks for myself nor for others, just that if given the choice and time, I would find reading more enjoyable. That is the critical aspect of both audiobooks and written literature, that ideally both should be available as a choice for people all around the world. In “Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports," Cody J. McDavis writes: “Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games). But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni. A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford."

Do you find his argument persuasive? What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?

---

In my opinion, this argument is a sound base, but is only half of the picture. I think college athletes should be paid - they are essentially working for their schools, and should be compensated as other student workers are. 
TThat said, te argument that paying college athletes would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni is a valid one.
 Or rather, that it could hurt students, schools, etc. It doesn't have to. It would be complicated, but rules, limits, and regulations could be developed to prevent or solve most of the issues that would arise from paying student athletes.

It could be argued that it is inherently unfair - that some sports are more popular than others, and that some schools have more money than others. Which is true. But some schools already have more money than others, better teams than others, and have other advantages. And the same with students - some are just better athletes and are highly courted already.

It seems unfair to take advantage of students talents and not compensate them. Yes, certain athletes in popular sports will make more money, and certain schools will be more desirable than others. But tht is post-school life anyway - graduates with degrees from "better"  schools have an easier time finding better, higher paying jobs, and student athletes from schools with strong programs are more likely to go on to be professional athletes. 

In fact, allowing college athletes to be paid, with oversight and a number of regulations, might help cut down on the unofficial and rather shady system of perks that is now used, making the whole system much more transparent and accountable. More attention would be paid to what students are actually receiving, and with caps might actually be fairer to all students. 

So, I believe there are a number of issues with paying student athletes, but there are also a lot of issues with the current system. Paying athletes like any other employee would allow a more fair system that could be regulated and monitored, and withg teh right rules could benefit everyone.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?

What stereotypical characters in books, movies or television shows make you cringe and why? Would you ever not watch or read something because of its offensive portrayal of someone?

---

In my opinion, stereotypes by themselves are not always harmful, as they are simply a shortcut that people make when they do not have enough information about an individual.  However, even though they are not intended to be harmful, they often can be, especially to the person who is being judged.  
I cringe when I see a character that is a stereotype because it makes me feel like the author is lazy., but I also feel that this use of stereotyping might end up being harmful to the group that the author is writing about.  For example, if an author writes about black youths who end up committing crimes, this would further strengthen society's expectations that young black males are violent, and this will lead others not to trust them.  Clearly, this is not right, because crime comes from poverty, not from race.  
I wwas fortunate in life to have been born a white male, which gives me definite advantages.  However, if I was a member of a minority group, I ould nprefer ot wto atch or read something that is offensive to me, because I would feel like the author is being disrespectful to me.
  I would also feel that I was rewarding this conduct on the part of authors and screenwriters, which would further encourage it.  

As a member of the majority, though, I do still cringe when I see minority groups portrayed in an insensitive, stereotypical fashion on TV, in movies, and to a lesser extent in books.  This not only harms the group as a whole, but it also affects individual actors.  When there are no roles available for minority actors except for those that perpetuate stereotypes, these actors are either left without opportunities, or they have to betray their morals in order to keep working.  

If people were more apt to reject stereotypes, these difficult decisions would not have to be made.  

Stereotypes do not always have to be negative, however.  Someone might assume that a young Asian person is smart, especially at math, or that someone who wears glasses is a good student.  They might assume that Native Americans are noble in spirit, or that elderly African Americans are devoted to family values.  These are all stereotypes that appear from time to time in fictional characters, and I have to object to them as well.

I generally do not have a severe negative reaction to these stereotypes, because I do not see any acute harm that comes from them, but they are still lazy.  One should not assume that the circumstances of one's birth have any impact on their character or their abilities.  After all, if you automatically assume that an Asian student is going to be the best in the class, aren't you also assuming that the other students are naturally inferior, because of their race?
ISo, in summary,  do not think that it is wrong to have a stereotype,.b This is something that happens automatically within our brains, and we can't really stop these thoughts from popping up.  Bt I think that it is wrong to judge someone based on a
 stereotype that either comes from within, or that we have picked up from society at large.  

Not only do stereotypes lead to negative judgments against others, which sometimes have real-world consequences, but they also prevent people from enjoying the kinds of equal opportunities that all of us deserve.  

The stereotype may be inevitable, but the prejudice that it leads to comes about by choice.  And that is a choice that no one should be making.
