If they were not to be able to use the sport to get their adrenaline, i am sure they would just find another place to do it. While it can of course be very risky to do these types of activities, it is that person's choice at the end of the day. People are going to have the freedom to make their own choices regardless, and unless the mountain itself is closed down for climbing, i would assume people would engage in the activity. I think this can also give people a lot of fullfillment through the sport, and this in turn makes them a better person. People need a little risk in their lives sometimes to feel alive. If they have to climb a mountain to get their kick, or ride on a bike or skateboard really fast, why not let them do it? I am just not a big proponent on restricting anyones choice in this way, as long as they are not forcing other people to do the same activity or putting anyone into danger. Something like climbing, is an individual activity. If that person was to make the choice to go and do it, why not let them try? How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, the reasoning that existed before the pandemic should still apply. Namely that screen time should be monitored, and that limiting your screen time is best for both mental and physical health. 
The science shows that too much screen time contributes to obesity, diabetes and hypertension.
 It can cause eye strain, disrupt your mental state, and alter your sleep patterns. That last one is very important, as uninterrupted sleep is an absolute requirement for fighting viruses and to speed up our healing responses. If there is one good thing that has come out of the pandemic it is increased awareness of health, and a new focus on maintaining and improving health. Limiting screen time is an important part of this. 

This is not to say that we should give up on screen altogether. They are an important tool for work efficiency, social connection, and overall entertainment. The main point is a balance must be found.
Do you think you're spending too much time on your screen?
 Then you probably are. Like anything else, technology can become excessive and unhealthy if not properly moderated. Exploring other alternatives in cases where screen related activities have taken over can help you learn where screens are essential to you, and where you could give them up (or use them less) for alternatives. 

In short, studies have shown that screen time can affect you physical and mental health, so treat screen time like you would anything else that can affect you health. Monitor and examine how it effects you. List the benefits and negatives , and you will be able to discover what you can do to integrate screen use into your life while minimizing any health effects. And keep up to date with new studies and new technologies; you may learn things which cause you to re-evaluate your current usage. And above all else; don't rely on screentime activities to provide you with everything (work, entertainment, social interaction). Variety is always the healthiest choice.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?

In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news? Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world? Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all? Why do you think the way you do?

---

In my opinion, it depends on what the news tells us. These days, the internet, the radio, the TV, and the newspapers are full of terrible news, unfortunately. So it depends on what, if anything, we can do about this news. I would argue that things such as COVID news are important to pay attention to, so that we can know what is safe to do and how we can protect others. Other news can be very important, but also deeply distressing to read, and knowing the information doesn't actually allow us to help other people. When it becomes important is when it comes to what we share, and how we participate civically.

There is so much misinformation out there, that we should be informed when we choose to share a fact or opinion. That is the least we can do. Plus, if we see a dubious-looking claim, it is up to us to get the correct information and correct the person. Furthermore, when it comes time to go into a voting booth, we need to be filled with good, true information.
There are cases where we would be bad citizens if we aren't up to date on world happenings.
 Especially if we're an undecided voter, or if there's a crisis unfolding where we can personally have a true impact. Don't get me wrong, it's generally important to be up to date on what is happening in the world. But for the sake of our own mental state, it can be helpful to filter what we take in. Do we need to know the latest guidelines from the CDC? 100%. Do we need to know the details of a presidential summit in Europe? Less so. Once again, this is good information to know, but there is so much news out there that we not only should not be expected to always be completely on top of it, but we also should feel free to not absorb every morsel of it.
People think that if they don't keep up with the news, then other people will think less of them.
 But I think the issue lies more with making sure to get correct and complete information before forming an opinion, and living your life based upon truth. As long as I have knowledgeable opinions based on objective facts, I will be able to participate in a democracy, I will be able to advocate for what I believe in, and I will be able to contribute to my society. 

Another situation where it is indeed important to be up to date on the news is when it comes to having perspective. Realizing where one stands in the world. For example, recent news from Afghanistan should cause people to feel strong empathy for the people there, and recognize their privilege, if not there, to be living in a place that is not under Taliban rule. One need not necessarily pore over every detail, but we should be informed enough to be compassionate.

In conclusion, we don't need every bit of news out there. And we need to filter what we take in, making sure to only draw from reliable sources. But we can also accept how overwhelming the 24-hour news cycle can be, and realize that we don't need to know every single thing that's happening. We can still be well informed, without being exhausted. Just make sure you always have a grip on reality, and are well informed on what matters for you to be a good citizen.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, screens are a clear and present danger in our lives. Despite this, screen use remains a necessary component of daily life. Because of this, we must remain more vigilant now than ever before about the potential negative impacts that it has on our daily lives. 

During the pandemic, the excessive screen use is resulting in lasting harm to health of our vision. This increase in usage often the result of sharp increases rather than a slow transition and is therefore more detrimental in the impact it has on our vision. Blue light has been linked to decreased retinal activity and has shown a statistically significant increase of early onset blindness in senior citizens who have reported more than 10 hours of screen time each day. 

Physical dangers aside, there is also a concern about the content that is behind the screen. We live in a time when truth and lies are blended together for our online consumption. This sharing of misinformation during a time when it is most important to have the best information possible has been extremely damaging to society’s trust in our institutions. Any benefits gained are far outweighed by the risk to our relationships and to the stability of our society.

Despite all of this, screens use is not likely to change and we should therefore make sure to protect our eyesight as best we can. It would also benefit our choices by better understanding the dangers and risks attached with prolonged screen use. In many ways, screens are such an important part of life that their use should be an assumed and any risks mitigated.

A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out. She’s unaware that she’s actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who’s fallen for her, and is certain he’s going to get it right this time.

One day, a man looked at himself in the mirror. “I’m not the man I want to be. And I can't seem to keep the woman I love. What am I going to do?”

The thing was, he had a pretty good idea of what he needed to do, he just wasn't sure it was the right thing to do.
The man was a shapeshifter.
 And over the years he had used his abilities to change his identity several times - whenever he missed out on a big job because of a bad interview, when he had gotten in trouble with the law, and yes, even with women. But when he had met Kara he decided he needed to change. She was the first person who had given him confidence in a long time. And he was certain he wanted to be with her forever. But after a little while, she started to notice things about him that he had wanted to hide. And she seemed to pull away from him. And last night, she broke up with him and said she didn't want to see him any more, that he wasn't the man she thought he was when they met.
He didn't need to be a mind reader to know what was going on.
 She was right, he wasn't the man she thought he was. So now the choice, did he change his face and try to be the man she wanted, or just let her go.
He looked at himself in the mirror again, and he made his decision.
 Not that it was ever really in question. And his eyes changed color, he grew and inch, and dozens of other changes happened. And then he started planning.

The first time they met again was at the library. She was looking for a book, and he was looking for her. And they chatted, and hit it off, just like the last time. And again they started dating. And he told her about his plans for the future, and she listened, and seemed to like what he had in mind. But again, after about 6 months, she broke up with him, with the same "You're not the man I thought you were."

The next time, he went for a little less attractive, a little more cuddly. And it was at the supermarket they met. He really thought he had it that time, but after only a few months she started saying they should see other people. 
He was getting frustrated.
 And even angry at her. One more time - the most attractive form he had ever taken, with all of the right words and gifts and thoughtfulness. But this time, even after weeks of being nice and approaching her in all the right ways, she wouldn't even accept a date with her.

"Kara, why won't you go out with me," he cajoled. "We'd be so perfect together!" 

Kara looked at him from across the table in the coffee shop they were in. "Chris, it's just...I don't know. I feel like I know you so well, and we share so many things, but it also feels completely wrong. I can't even imagine dating you." She looked away, with an awkward expression. "I'm sorry, but if you are  going to keep pushing, I don't think we should be friends."

He stood up in a rage, finally losing all of his cool and caution. "What do you mean by that. After all of these years and all of the work I've done to be perfect and you won't even listen to me!"

Kara was certain he was having a breakdown. Maybe that was why all of her internal warnings not to date him had been going off? "Chris, calm down. I said I feel like I've known you forever, but it has only been a few weeks.,,"

Suddenly, as she looked at him, his face and body morphed. From one familiar form to another, until finally he became the man she had met years ago. The man she still loved, but wasn't sure he could trust. And now she knew why.

She stood up, and ran away. As he ran after her, he tripped and fell into the street. By the time he got up and out of the way of traffic she was gone. And, as his rage faded he knew that this time he needed to let her go. He thought of the terror and betrayal he had seen in her eyes the moment before she ran. It finally broke his heart. He changed shape and walked away again. And this time he just kept walking.

Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?

---

In my opinion, it is absolutely a must that we consider extreme sports like mountain climbing to be real sports. We have gone too far in our obsession with safety and in this case I think we have stopped athletes from achieving their full potential. Anyone going in with any dangerous sports already have learned about the risks and dangers associated with it, so why be overly cautious?

It's on you, the athlete who fail to prepare or neglect to respect risks, not the organizers who incorporate safety measures. It's also not on spectators that have paid, and paid a great deal of money to go support and watch the athletes do what they love. It's on you, the athlete who failed to get any sort of life insurance to keep their loved ones protected just in case of the unlikely event of an accident happening.

If we don't consider sports like mountain climbing, parachuting, skydiving, running with the bulls, etc to be a real sport then it's going to be a sad day when we hit a patch of very mundane and very uninteresting sports. What are we going to watch instead? E-sports? Where "athletes" are just sitting on their computer and mouse and keyboard and doing absolutely nothing except for playing a video game? We hear those commentators say things like, "the character killed about 15 people in one match," and we call that a sport? Just give me a break.

I know I sound a little bit angry, but wouldn't you be? I've read our history books when there were no safety involved and people just went all in, doing whatever they felt like doing. We did not get stories about plain old men dying of chest injuries incurred during sports because the protective chest plates was too heavy to come with them everywhere, or protectors were not available, no. We heard stories of mighty men overcoming their fears and coming out on top. Stories like those helped shape our culture, and those stories are sometimes what we want to emulate. Stories of overcoming something despite the odds or because of the odds, that's what makes for a powerful tale. If we stopped trying, if we stopped taking risks or stopped offering them, then aren't we depriving ourselves of knowing what the meaning of challenge really is?

If our mentality is focused on safety, we would not have gotten to the moon, we would not have airplanes, we would not have cellphones, and the world would be a pretty boring place because people took it safe. So if you're me, I dare welcome extreme sports, because if we don't, we're going to end up losing a lot in the process.

Should Schools Provide Free Pads and Tampons?

Have you ever experienced period shaming, or “period poverty”? Should schools step in to help? Should schools be required to provide free pads and tampons to students? How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools? How are they different?

---

In my opinion, schools are ideally responsible for the safety, health, welfare and formal education of young people. Unfortunately, many school districts barely have funding to provide education, leaving absolutely nothing for considerations of health and welfare of the children. And that doesn't even factor in the other things that schools are responsible for (building maintenance, transportation of students and special needs children, etc.

The short answer is yes, schools should be providing everything that any and all students may need, throughout the school day. Unfortunately, the text above isn't an opinion piece, and so the short answer, though likely correct, is rather unsatisfying. It is disingenuous to suggest that schools should provide more material resources than they are afforded by their communities. The slightly longer and much sadder answer is, yes they should provide such resources to students, if they can afford to do that. That is not ideal, but it is the reality faced by school administrators.

The problem of sanitary napkins in schools cannot be addressed without first addressing the broader social issue of community expenditures. Communities decide how to allocate funds, and until they allocate a sufficient amount to the school systems that serve their children, the schools are not, ultimately, to blame for a lack of resources. That said, it is the school administrators’ responsibility to find creative ways to be responsive to vulnerable populations within their districts. There needs to be a renewed interest in renaissance values to get the necessary funding and there needs to be accountability, from an administrative point of view, for how the funds are used. It's a multi-faceted problem that begins with voter mindset.

There can be no simple solution to this problem. For now, administrators will have to do the best they can with what they have.

When you're 28, science discovers a drug that stops all effects of aging, creating immortality. Your government decides to give the drug to all citizens under 26, but you and the rest of the “Lost Generations" are deemed too high-risk. When you're 85, the side effects are finally discovered.

After all of these years, all of the tests and reports, they had finally found something wrong with the drug. But you couldn't help but feel like there was more to it. Why had it taken so long for side effects to show up? And why were they affecting both people who had taken the drug nearly 50 years ago and those who had taken it less than 10 years ago. At the same time? It didn't make sense to you. 
You were still trying to figure it out when you got the call.
 An old friend of yours - well, weren't they all old now? - called you up and asked you to meet with her. "Don't tell anyone" she said. And you didn't.

You met her at an old restaurant, one stilled owned by another of the Lost Generations. "I need to tell you something." she said. "It's probably going to be hard to hear." She took a deep breath and looked at you, the wrinkles on her face deep with concern. "These side effects aren't side effects of the drug. They are 'side effects' of government policy."

"What!" 

"Shhh" she said. "You must remain calm. We're can't take any risks right now." 
"What are you talking about?
" you tried to remain calm, but judging by her face it was not a good performance. 
"The side effects are the result of policy.
 Think about it, if everyone lives forever the planet can't sustain us all for long. So when the population reaches a certain point, they hold a lottery." She covered her mouth after she said it, as if there was a possibility one of the other patrons would hear.

Oh god, you suddenly understood. It was population control, and anyone who wasn't going to die naturally was a possible target. You suddenly thought about what a crime it was to have the government decide who lives and who dies.

"So, what do we do?" you asked. 

"Well, we're still trying to figure that out. But I have to warn you, you're not going to like what the most likely plan is." 
"I'll do whatever it takes." you said without hesitation.


She looked at you with steely eyes. "I am part of a group who foresaw this plan decades ago. We've been infiltrating the system at every level, every department, every related company. And we do have a plan. To be honest I lied just now, we know what has to be done. We don't need you, I just wanted to...warn you."
"What is the plan?"
 

She looked at you. We are going to destroy the ability to create the drug, all current supplies, and all information related to the drug. It will no longer be available. Soon, and from now on, all humanity will live normal life spans, just like you and I will. Except for those who have already taken the drug."
"What about them?" you weren't sure you could go along with the plan.


She looked somber. "They will die eventually too, rather through accident, suicide, or just neglect. Unfortunately they will have to see many of their younger relatives and friends die. But it is necessary to avoid this dystopian future for all."
You had to admit it made sense.
 You hated it. But... your children and grandchildren didn't have the "side effects" yet; if this meant they could make their own choices in the future, it was worth it.

You went home and kept silent. You told no one of your conversation. And then one day the news came that the drug had been destroyed. Everyone was horrified, since the fact of the government's "policy" wasn't revealed. The conspirators decided that it was best faith in the government remained. It was necessary if they were to avoid a bloody revolution. 

Eventually, using some clever social engineering, they were able to spread the idea that losing the drug and the "side effects" was for the best. People accepted it. And you took the secret to the grave, content with the hope for a better future.

In my opinion, pads and tampons are a necessity in just the same way as toilet paper, soap, and so on. In fact, not providing them is arguably a case of sex discrimination, since all other essentials are supplied. In addition, for school students, puberty is a time when they are still adjusting to needing these supplies, and they may not be prepared. The supplies need to be available conveniently. 
In addition, it is not just a matter of convenience.
 This is a health issue, because the ability to have clean sanitary supplies can help to prevent infections. Since schools are invested in helping students have basic good health in other ways, such as providing a nurse's office, it makes sense to provide a cleanliness necessity just as they supply toilet paper. 

The main way that pads and tampons are different is that only one group needs them. But this does not argue against providing the supplies. Since it is a biological basic necessity, it is not a matter of choice. The same is true for toilet paper, soap, and other products. This really means that not providing these supplies is ignoring a group's basic needs while needs that apply to all students are supplied. It also suggests that those making these types of decisions were not thinking about it and not consulting with those who use the bathrooms. 

To suggest that money is an issue here is to miss the point, because if the school can afford to supply other basic necessities such as indigestion medicine, toilet paper, soap, hand dryers, and tylenol, then pads and tampons fall into the same category and should be paid for from the same budget. School students also have to rely on adults for at least most of their money, since they cannot be employed if they are under the employment age, and if they are old enough to work they cannot work more than 20 hours per week. Many students' families cannot afford everything they need and rely on the school to meet them partway by providing basic needs during the school day. In conclusion, yes, school should supply sanitary products for students.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?

Do you listen to audiobooks? What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading? Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening? Which method do you prefer? Why?

---

In my opinion, the primary difference between listening and reading is the level of interaction one has with the book. 
When you read, you are the one creating the images in your head.
 The pace is your own. The descriptions, the tone, the characters' voices, all are part of your creation. Your emotions and actions are very much your own.   You are both a reader and a participant in the story. You decide how much, if at all, you interact with the characters and both their conversations and actions.

When you are listening to an audiobook, your level of interaction is very different.   Instead of creating the images for yourself, you are using the reader's voice and intonations to create a mental picture. The mood, tone, inflections, and interpretation have already been done for you by the voice artist. You are a listener, rather than a player. The voice artist is the one creating a mental picture for you, taking away the ability to create your own. 
There are some levels in which this can be good.
 For instance, you may not be able to read because you are visually impaired and cannot see the words. Or if you struggle with a short attention span or problems focusing, listening may work better for you. Or perhaps you simply don't like reading, or it is just more convenient to listen.  One downside of listening is that you cannot speed up or slow down the voice artist's reading. It is even possible that you might dislike the voice of the narrator, which makes it impossible to listen to. 

Either way,   listening to a book can give you a similar experience of reading, and it is great for encouraging children to read. In the end, whether you read or listen to a book, just make time for the one you love!

McDavis writes: “Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games). But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni. A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford."

Do you find his argument persuasive? What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?

---

College athletes are in many ways comparable to athletes older than them, that participate in professional leagues outside of colleges and universities. Many of college athletes put in tremendous amount of effort and their time to improve their abilities, and to seek achievement of the sport of their choosing. This effort and time is primarily reflected in the outcomes of the sport for the colleges they are associated with, whether it is the games they win for their teams, or the records they may break in other types of sports. 
College athletes are also in many ways comparable to other students, who are not athletes.
 They still have educational obligations to meet apart from the demands of the sport, which in too can conflict with work demands if they hold one. Having to juggle a variety of obligations in a day can be tiring and stressful, which impacts the performance of a college athlete much like any other type of athlete. However, the college athletes that are not paid to the same degree as professional athletes like in the MLB, NFL, NHL, and much more will no doubt be subjected to much more stressors from the lack of finances. 
The argument that college athletes should not be paid ithat is ased on the idea that the current system of scholarships and other benefits is enough. is a flawed line of thinking. That is assuming that college athletes like other students, don't accumulate debt through other expenses apart from the ones necessary to pay for their education. Scholarships and other benefits are sufficient to pay for tuition and the cost of materials, but like other students, many of college athletes have other areas to attend to. This includes living arrangements, food, hobbies, and much more than will be difficult to pay for with scholarships and other benefits, more so for some than others. College athletes often will struggle between their obligations to make money if they aren't being paid for their efforts in the sport, given that a part-time or even full-time job is difficult enough for students with educational demands. Paying them like other athletes will help them meet the demands of their finances as it relates to their education, personal life, and their sport.
The argument that paying college athletes would ruin the sport is also flawed., given that such a concept exist in professional leagues and other sports. Universities benefit much from college athletes, more so from the ones that have high prestige, performance, and reputation. The bidding wars and other excessive costs that universities pay for their athletes are in part of their own vocation, something that can be prevented through more regulation, and effecitvely the fair treatment of all college athletes for their efforts. These can be reduced so that the university will not impact other students, while still being able to pay athletes for their efforts that is necessary for them to continue their sports career, while also furthering their educational career.

The game ends when the last card is drawn from the stack.
 The player with the most Mana wins. If the game is being played in tournament mode, then the winning mana goes into the collective pot, and is divided up between the players before the start of the next game.

What Are the Most Important Things Students Should Learn in School?

In your opinion, what are the most important things students should learn in school? What is the most important thing you have learned in school? How has this knowledge affected your life? How do you think it will help your success in the future?

---

In my opinion, the most important purpose of school is not to learn concrete things (though this is definitely important, as well) but rather to learn how to learn.   I think that the most important thing I have learned in school is how to learn, even though I didn't really know it at the time, and this skill has stayed with me throughout my life.  If I had applied myself more strongly in school, I would probably be doing much better.

There is a common argument than in the internet age, people don't really need to learn facts, because we can easily find the answers to questions.  However, I think this idea is misguided.  School is necessary to teach students a foundation of knowledge, so that they can know what questions they need to be asking.  For this reason, knowing basic mathematics, and also the fundamentals of grammar, history, the scientific method, and the humanities are vitally important for everyone.  

Someone can easily find out what year the Battle of Hastings took place, but without attending school and paying sufficient attention, they wouldn't know that such a thing was important, nor would they have any idea why it was a topic of discussion.  I think that by learning how to learn, I can continue to expand my own breadth of knowledge, and to deal with unexpected new problems, simply because I recognize facts and techniques that I had used before.  Obviously, no one can remember everything, but a good education can remind us of what we need to know, and thus, make it easy to figure it out again.  

However, I also think that there are some very important subjects that are not being taught in school, and I wish that I had learned these things when I was young.  
WSome of he most important things sthat tudents should learn in school?, include media literacy and skeptical thinking.  Kids (and adults) need to learn how to evaluate claims that are made by pundits, by journalists, and by advertisers.  Many of the current problems our country faces would be alleviated if people had simply gained the ability to recognize when they are being lied to.  

Another important topic that should be taught in school is personal finance, accounting, and law.  Students leave school without enough practical knowledge, and oftentimes, their parents lack this knowledge as well.  As I said before, a child with a good fundamental education can teach him or herself how to deal with practical problems in life, but it would be much easier if they were taught this kind of thing in school.  If I had my way, "Home Economics" would be brought back and taught every year, and it would teach students about all the practical issues they will face at home, including economics, maintenance, car repair, budgeting, and so on.  

Alas, I am starting to get off topic, so I will return to my main point.  The most important thing you can learn in school is how to learn.  If you know the basics of the research process, and also know enough basic facts to recognize how complicated most problems are, you can probably figure out the rest for yourself.  I think it took me well into my college years to be able to say that I finally understood these things, and sadly, many students will not have that same opportunity.  And that is why I think that schools should concentrate on fundamentals, but also on pragmatics.  

I hope that future generations will be taught how to teach themselves to deal with unique problems, but I also hope that they will be taught exactly how to deal with the most common problems.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, we should be worried about the excessive screen time during the Pandemicfor two reasons.
 irst, we have no idea what the long-term effects of excessive screen time are.
 The obvious bad effect is that the screen time deprives us of the actual social contact with our family members, friends and coworkers. We can't feel the closeness with our loved ones, nor can we hug them to show our affection. We can't share a meal with them, or play with our kids. The second reason is that screen time distracts us from the real world. We are so busy with our screens that we don't notice what is going on around us. We don't notice the people who are sick and need help. We don't notice the people who are in need of a hug, or who are lonely and need a friend. We also lack the time to get enough physical exercise. Screen time is in no way a substitute for actual contact with other human beings. Thus, we should be worried about the excessive screen time and avoid it to a certain extent.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, we should be both worried about excessive screen time, but also glad that the pandemic did not hit so early that we would be denied the chance to use our screens in this fashion.  
I am worried about screen time bin general, not just during the pandemic, ecause I believe that it is a major factor in the epidemic of childhood obesity and the rise in childhood diabetes.
  This is, of course, also a factor of portion sizes and the increasing amounts of sugar and fat that are included in convenience foods that are marketed toward children.  Given that most families have two working parents, and some of them have more than one job, we cannot pass judgment on families for this outcome.  They simply do not have the time to cook at home or to engage in vigorous exercise with their children.  If screens were not so enticing to children (perhaps, because we lived in an earlier time) or because parents were deliberately denying their children screen time, then it is possible that they would play outside more often.  This additional exercise would be good for their bodies and possibly their minds as well.  
I am also worried about screen time because of the potential for addiction.
  Video games and social media are almost tailor-made to feed out brain's desire for feedback and stimulation, and it can be hard to drag ourselves away from devices that give us what we want.  

Although these trends are worrying, we have to accept the world as it is, and there is little that we can do to change other people's behavior unless they themselves are willing to change.  This would require a mutual desire in both children and parents to limit their exposure to screens, and this perfect situation is rare.  

My broader point is that we should be worried about screen time, especially for children.  We should also be worried about the amount of time that we spend on our own screens, and we should try to limit our screen time as much as possible.  Social media and even video games can have the same effect on adult brains as they do on children.  Likewise, a sedentary lifestyle can be unhealthy for anyone, so we need to force ourselves to get up and move, preferably outside.  

When it comes to the pandemic, however, I think we have to accept that screens (while dangerous when over-used) are very helpful.  We need to be able to communicate with our families and friends, and we need to be able to access information about the virus.  Internet-connected devices may feed our addictions, but they also allow us to keep in touch with the people we care about.  If kids were playing outside with their friends, they might have spread the virus and caused much more loss of life than we have already seen.  And keeping kids indoors, in isolation, without any way to communicate would probably be worse for their long-term health than excessive socialization on the internet has been.  

And so, te bottom line is that we should be worried about screen time, but we should also be glad that the pandemic hit when it did.
  Screentime has been a crutch that has helped get us through a very difficult period in our lives and in our history.  However, whenever we are safely able to do so, we should try to return to a life in which interactions are sometimes made in person, and in which people interact in the real world.  It is healthier for us on so many levels to be active, social, and connected.  Once the acute risk of disease has passed, or has at least been controlled, we should try to get ourselves back out there.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?

In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news? Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world? Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all? Why do you think the way you do?

---

In my opinion, someone who does not keep up with the news is not a bad citizen, but they cannot call themselves a good and responsible citizen either.   n other words, Ithink that everyone has some responsibility to know what is going on in the world, but I do not think that it is a requirement. to call oneself a citizen.

The news ultimately affects all of us, whether directly, or indirectly through the political process.  We cannot make good decisions without being informed, so I think that it is important for any responsible citizen to follow events in the news and to understand the historical underpinnings of events.  

If one does not follow the news in the world, and does not therefore understand what is happening, they will be apt to make bad decisions that not only affect themselves, but could potentially be harmful for others as well.  Think of the people who refuse to listen to scientific fact about vaccines.  They are the reason why Covid-19 has not been controlled in the United States, despite the fact that we have ample access to vaccines.  This lack of information, or more seriously, abundance of false information, has been literally deadly to many.
However, I do not think that it is necessary for everyone to be a news junkie.
  I think that it is important to be informed, but I do not think that it is necessary to know every detail of every story.  In fact, spending too much time concentrating on current events can actually be harmful in itself, since it would distract from other pursuits.  Getting too bogged down in the minutiae of up-to-the-minute events can also lead to a poor understanding of the events themselves, since one will not be able to step back and see the history.  One would not be seeing the forest because the trees are in the way, as the old saying goes.

My opinion of the news media is not strictly positive, though.  Media outlets, at best, chase ratings or (in the case of public broadcasting) donations from members, and this can lead them to focus on eye-catching reporting at the expense of important reporting.  Very few news outlets spend much time on budgetary concerns in government, or distant ethnic tensions, because readers are not interested, but if this information was pushed to the forefront, it could be beneficial to everyone.  

In addition, we cannot pretend that the news media is impartial and unbiased.  All persons are biased toward a certain viewpoint, and this bias can become entrenched when journalists have to please college professors and later editors who all tend to feel the same way.  When alternative media outlets pop up, they end up pushing brainless conspiracy theories instead of giving fact-based rebuttals to biases at other sources, because this is what their viewers want to hear.  And even when they act responsibly, highly partisan news sources often take an extreme position, even when they back it up with facts and evidence.  
In conclusion, I think that everyone has some responsibility to be informed about the world around them, but I do not think that it is necessary
 (or even wise) for them to spend the majority of their time on the news.  In addition, they need to be skeptical about what they hear in the news media, but even more skeptical about people who claim that the media are always wrong.  Finally, responsible citizens need to not only follow the news, but also try to get a deeper understanding of what led to current events.  Some of the time spent reading the newspapers would be better spent reading a book that chronicles the full story of a recent, or current, event.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?

Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten? Or that other researchers found that if forced to choose, 40 percent of people would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist.

Why do you think many people are more empathetic toward the suffering of animals than that of people? In your opinion, is it wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering? Why do you think so?

---

In my opinion, being outraged about what goes through the heads of others is an unproductive way to do activism. At the end of the day, it's not about what people think, it's about what they do. While 40 percent of people may have said they would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist, it's another matter entirely what they would do in real life if faced in that situation. 
The fact is, most people don't want to think about the suffering of others. at all, whether they're human or animal or even a plant. Humans are emotional and sympathetic creatures, with a vibrant capacity to feel pain; thus, we will often do anything to avoid those feelings of pain. It's important to recognize that it can often be easier for a human to ruminate on the suffering of an animal as opposed to the suffering of a fellow human, because the animal is more distant to us and therefore harder to empathize with completely. This doesn't necessarily speak to any given human's true morality, but rather their emotional coping mechanisms when faced with difficult moral questions.

The question of whether it's wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering is a fallacious one. In fact, activists can care about multiple causes at once; it's not a zero-sum game. Much in the same way that somebody can care about ending homelessness and ending racism, somebody else can care about protecting animals and protecting humans. There's never anything wrong with caring, because caring about something does not preclude the possibility of caring about other things, whether they're "worthy" causes or not. Suggesting that one group (or species, as it were) is more important and worthy than another is simply a way to divide people who could otherwise be driven to unite over the same cause. Instead of a world where people have to choose between animals and humans, why not a world where everybody cares about both?

Animals and humans are both worthy of our empathy, and it's important to recognize that. Life itself is precious, and we should all be working together to protect it. While "working together" may not necessarily mean volunteering hands-on at a farm or attending the same pro-rights protest, it does mean respecting the decisions that each individual makes about where to devote their time, energy and compassion. Our job as activists isn't to spy over the shoulder of our neighbors, waiting for them to slip up or have the wrong priorities, but to support each other in the causes that we all care about. There's nothing wrong with caring about both animals and people too, because at the end of the day, the most important thing is that we care at all.

A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford."

Do you find his argument persuasive? What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?

---

In my opinion, the opinion presented by McDavis is broadly appealing, but it ignores key facts about what is already happening in college sports.  Top universities are already paying for a select few athletes, but they are doing so with perks and special treatment that ultimately does not benefit those students in the same way that fair payment for service would.  
The NCAA is a monopoly that has no incentive to change the way it operates., and sadly, there is practically a requirement that aspiring professional athletes must compete on the NCAA's terms.  

It would be great if college sports could live up to the ideal of scholars who compete as a hobby and as a way to show pride in their universities, but this is clearly not the case in reality.  College is viewed as a stepping stone by a lucky few who feel that they have what it takes to make a career out of playing sports.  They are generally given special treatment by professors who view the sports teams as a vital part of the university's balance sheet, and often are not held to the same standards as other students.  

And we should not judge the players themselves too harshly for this system, because they did not make the rules.  The NCAA and the colleges require them to work more than full time at their sport, all for the good of the school.  They do not have time to pursue a full-time education and to work to support themselves.
The NCAA's rules argainst paying these players ae designed to protect the interests of the universities and the NCAA itself, not the players.
  This means that college sports attracts only those who have the financial wherewithal to attend college while essentially doing nothing but training and competing in sports, all for the hoped-for reward of a professional sports contract after graduation.  This is not what the college athletic ideal hoped for, and we should stop pretending that those ideals are being upheld.

If we accept reality, on the other hand, and pay athletes for their service, then they can pursue their education either part time or after they have competed to their own satisfaction.  As it currently stands, however, we are just forcing student athletes to work for their institutions for nothing more than a vague promise of future riches.  This is not fair, and it is not right.

No matter how you look at it, this is either a violation of labor laws, or it is a violation of the NCAA's stated ideal of the scholarly athlete.  Nobody can, and nobody should, accept the system in its current form.  Giving students housing allowances and other forms of compensation is just a disguised form of payment, so why do we pretend that a paycheck would change anything?

I contend that the college-athletics system has evolved, and that if people are happy with the way it is set up, then the employees who are keeping it going should be paid fairly for their efforts.  If any coaches or talent scouts disagree, then I would invite them to give up their salaries and instead work for the same promises that they give to their students.

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, we should embrace the benefits of our digital devices.
The benefits of screen time are many.
 In terms of education for our children, the use of computers and zoom and programming geared towards kids was the only thing for many schools that allowed them to teach at all the 2020-2021 school year. Without technology and computer use, millions of children would have had absolutely no way to be in contact with their teachers and get even a semblance of learning. The use of zoom classroom allowed teachers to visually see their students and for the kids in the classes to interact with their educator and each other.

Another advantage, speaking again in terms of children, that I have noticed is when my kids are playing multiplayer games online. The ones I am most familiar with are Roblox and Overwatch.  My children have made friends from all around the world while playing these games. One always has to be vigilant for online predators, and to educate children about being safe online, but the knowledge of other cultures and other countries my children have gained with communicating with youngsters from varied areas is immeasurable. For youth to be able to interact with diverse people in a situation where you have to help each other to survive, can't really be taught in life outside a gaming situation. 

 have also noticed that my children are much more comfortable with technology than I was at their agee. I could barely figure out how to turn a computer on when I was 12, let alone program or do research. I have to ask my 12 year old for help with word sometimes, and my older teen with power point.  As with anything in this life, moderation and discipline are key. This actually another benefit. The advantages are obvious to me and technology should be embraced and utilized as the tool it is.

Should Schools Provide Free Pads and Tampons?

How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools? How are they different?

---

While I have not personally experienced period shaming or period poverty, I have witnessed such incidents first hand when I attended high school, and middle school as well. I think it is a negative outcome for female students, that personally affects them psychologically, and for a long period of time. Ideally , girls should be able to buy and receive whatever products they might need for their menstruation without any worry. Schools should step in and help this natural process of life that female students go through. For many students, it can be a daunting endeavor to understand the process of which pads or tampons to buy. For others, poverty can affect whether they can buy menstrual process on a constant and regular basis. Thus, providing free pads and tampons can help limit the period shaming, and period poverty that female students are regularly subject to.

Tampons and Pads are much similar to Band-Aids and similar items provided by the school. For example, they are hygienic items like soap and toilet paper, intended to make the user clean and avoid appearing unhygienic. Like Band-Aids, they stop bleeding for a period of time and as long as one continues to wear them, and they have to be changed out every while. I am sure that students would appreciate seeing them in the school, just as they would any other supply readily available in school. However, unlike Band-Aids and other items, their ought to be a better sense of privacy for the students requesting tampons and pads. For example, there should not be any announcement in an auditorium or over the intercom that the student need pads or tampons, and ideally the school would not keep a record of such, allowing the students to remain anonymous when requesting the pads and receiving them. Through that, they can receive the tampons and pads they require, without feeling judged for doing so and potentially being stigmatized for what is effectively a natural and commonplace occurrence. 

Schools ought to be a place where students feel comfortable and able to learn and develop as individuals. Providing tampons and pads are a critically way for schools to do so for female students. By offering them in a private and respectful way, schools can give comfort and stability for students undergoing their period, that otherwise might be judged and ridiculed for lacking access to such supplies.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?

What stereotypical characters in books, movies or television shows make you cringe and why? Would you ever not watch or read something because of its offensive portrayal of someone?

---

In my opinion, stereotypes that are portrayed in works of fiction are generally not intended to be harmful, and may come about unconsciously, but they do exacerbate feelings that lead to discrimination against, and sometimes direct harm to, marginalized groups in society.  For this reason, I would generally prefer not to watch or read something that revels in stereotypes, but sometimes I endure such things because of the cultural or entertainment value.  I suspect that if I was a member of a marginalized group, or was otherwise directly affected, I might take a stronger stance against such works. 

I hrve already written at length about how I feel about stereotypes in general, so for today, I would like to talk about some of te most egregious instances of stereotyping in ymyreading or viewing experiences?.  
Please note that in all cases, I am not claiming negligence on the part of the author.
  I cannot know or predict what the author truly had in mind, but I will allow for the possibility (nay, the probability) that the author was simply relaying feelings that he or she had picked up from society.  The fact that society felt this way is not the author's fault, but I still take exception to the fact that the author reinforces these feelings.

So, onto the business at hand, the most common and harmful stereotype I see is that of black people.  This goes back to the Jim Crow era in which African-Americans were portrayed as happy fools who loved to work on plantations, where they could dance and sing in the sunlight.  Needless to say, this was never true, but it made white audiences feel better about themselves.  In this one case, I think that the stereotype was indeed created from willful malice.  

Hattie McDaniels's character in Gone with the Wind is another example.  She is portrayed as someone who would be helpless if she was not enslaved by a rich white family, and we are meant to believe that she is grateful for what she received.  However, this is also an instance in which a black woman was humanized and portrayed fairly respectfully on screen, so I cannot totally object to it.  
For a far more serious example, let us consider the trope of the "black friend."
  This is often a character who is portrayed with no depth, and simply exists to make the main characters (who are almost always white) appear to be more tolerant and worldly.  A black friend simply exists to make the audience think that the white characters are more popular and universally appreciated.  At times, the black friend even ends up having some connection to the underworld, which the main characters can harmlessly exploit.  This is just as bad as explicitly claiming that all black people are involved in crime, because that is what the audience is led to believe.  
The only possible situation in which I would tolerate a stereotype is if it were dportrayedby an obviously ignorant character ,win a fictional setting, ho could not be expected to know
 any better.  This might actually be beneficial for society, because audiences who came to see a heroic white cast, might end up learning a subtle lesson about questioning the stereotypes that pervade our society.  

Unfortunately, I cannot readily think of an example in which I have seen this happen in fiction, and there have been far to many examples of harmful stereotypes.  I hope that the few examples which I had time to share were illustrative of the broader point.

When you die, you appear in a cinema with a number of other people who look like you. You find out that they are your previous reincarnations, and soon you all begin watching your next life on the big screen.

"Well," she thought "This sucks."

Jane sat in front of a large screen, with a dozen other people around her. Various genders, colors, ages. She looked around at the other people as they all watched life play out on the screen. She had always disliked the movies anyway, and now she was stuck here, with a movie she had no control over. With "herself"? Nope. Not what she had been hoping for. 
As the movie went on, Jane found herself not really watching.
 "Whatever. Is this some kind of reward? Watching someone else who will claim to be you, doing things you can't control? Or is this some kind of punishment?" Jane looked around, desperate for distraction. Another, older woman was sitting nearby. She saw Jane looking at her, and smiled. She decided to risk it. Was talking during a "movie" even bad manners in the afterlife anyway? 

"Hi. How long have you been here?" Jane whispered, still playing by the rules even in her frustration. 
"Oh, I've been here for a long time.
" The older woman smiled. "Longer than anyone else still here." 

Jane focused on her, and that statement. "What do you mean? How many of me have there been? More than this?"  
"Oh yes.
 But I don't think even in all that time that I ever really though of any of them as 'me'." "
Why are you still here?" It sounded like others were here, but now they are gone? Where?
 Jane asked, more loudly than she meant to.

Some of the others turned to look at her. Most looked lost, but some looked contemplative. And one in particular looked almost...satisfied. 

"Why are you so interested in them?" The older woman asked, growing tense as she looked at the one, satisfied looking person. "It's not like we are connected at all, other than being told we share a soul, which seems like nonsense to me given what I've seen on the screen!" 

The older woman seemed to be getting agitated, and as Jane split her attention between the screen, the older woman, and the satisfied looking person, something strange and amazing happened. She suddenly had a memory. Just like the young boy on the screen she had once broken a friend's toy and then tried to hide the evidence. But the boy on the screen then did something different - he changed his mind and confessed. The friend forgave him, and they both felt better. And suddenly the satisfied looking person (whom Jane had decided to call George) smiled, and just vanished. 

She watched George's departure, and noticed that even the older woman looked relieved. "Well, another one gone and I still don't know how they do it. But that was nice. I wish I had done that when I was a child."

Jane thought hard, she felt like some thought was just out of reach. Something that was a part of her memory, but not. "Wait, the same thing happened to you? Me too. I wonder if maybe, we are all more connected than you think."

The older woman frowned. "But we are all so different, just look at us." 

Jane looked at her, and thought about it. "Yes, but that is the outside. And anyway, isn't the whole idea to grow and change, and learn? Maybe that is the point? To learn? About ourselves? What we can do or be better?" 

Jane was surprised to realize that she felt excited and alive again. She grabbed the older woman's hand. "How about we watch the movie together, and see what else we can learn? Together, as one"

The older woman, relaxed, and moved closer to Jane. "Yes, you know, that sounds nice. Nothing has sounded so nice r exciting for so long."

And as the women watched the movie together, they talked. And shared, and learned. And as the movie came to an end they both looked quite satisfied, and vanished just as an old man appeared in the theater.

This seems so impossible. The queen of bees? But you are a person, right. You look at the tiny figure and ask him to explain. The bee says that you were found when you were very little by a family that took you in. You had been born a bee, and were a bee when you were found. Over time, however, as the human family nursed you to health, you became more and more human. By the time you had reached 2 years of age, you were completely in human form. You had no memory of your life as a bee, and the family had no memory of ever having found you. All they seemed to know was that they were afraid of bees. Johnson was shocked himself, finding it hard to gather the words the President wanted to hear. "I don't know sir...What did the Russians say?"

The President went even more pale. "Apparently there aren't "Russians" anymore. Just the West Asian Conglomerate."

 The Interior Minister of Return spoke up.  Shouted the President. "We just need to show them..."

Should College Athletes Be Paid?

Do you think college athletes should be paid? Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In “Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports," Cody J. McDavis writes: “Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games). But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni. A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford."

Do you find his argument persuasive? What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?

---

In my opinion, college athletes should be paid. Like any other worker, they are selling their bodies and selling a service; for that, they should be adequately compensated.

College athletes provide a service to their schools; they attract fans and prospective students, they generate revenue, and they make schools known, often on a national level. They are the face of their schools, and they are the ones who put in the time and effort to make their schools successful. This is also in addition to juggling courseloads, jobs, and other student activities. Any other student working for the university would get paid, up to and including the mascot, so why not the actual athletes themselves?
The NCAA is a multi-billion dollar industry, and it is not paying its workers.
 It's unfair to claim that paying athletes would cause financial issues for universities when those athletes bring in so much money in the first place. Raising ticket prices to sporting events would be one way to make up for the money that would be paid to athletes, for example. Another would be to pay athletes a standard wage much in the same way that other student staff are compensated; this would eliminate any risk of big universities buying star players.

Star collegiate athletes often go on to become professional players. If they will be paid for being in the big leagues, why not also pay them for the work that they do at a lower level? The NCAA is a stepping stone for these athletes, and it is unfair to them to not compensate them for their performance and efforts.

Even in athletics, the principles of workers' rights still apply. College athletes are not just students; they are entertainers, professionals, public figures, and ultimately workers. Their lives revolve around being in top physique so they can play for their universities the same way that major league players would. For this reason, they should absolutely be compensated and held in the same regard as anybody else who performs services of value.

You both process a host of visual, tactile, olfactory and other cues that we have evolved over millions of years to appreciate and understand. You might even notice the subtlety of another person’s breathing change, the difference in their skin where they broke their collar bone once and that has not fully healed.
When you have a screen between you, you can’t see any of this.
 In fact, if you've ever had the experience of finally meeting in real life a person you have digitally interacted with on many occasions, you probably have been struck by how little the person in front of you has to do with the mental construct you have formed from those digital sessions.
As screen time increases, people are disengaging from their loved ones and their communities.
 An app-mediated interaction is a pale shadow of what can transpire in even a 60-second meeting. Facebook "friends" have almost nothing to do with real friendship: they can be the result of real friendship, but are almost never the cause.

The more we screen, the less we actually communicate.  And the less we communicate, the fewer common values and ideas we share, and the more alienated we become from each other. 

And here's the thing. The less we communicate with each other, the more we are opening the door to a host of new digital communicable diseases: trolling, hacking, gaslighting, rumor-spreading, fake news, and much more. How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?

The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won. We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now? Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

---

In my opinion, we should be worried about excessive screen time during the pandemic.   Staring at electronic screens can have bad effects on our health.  Our eye health can be adversely affected by the increased screen time.  More screen time may cause us to get less sleep.  An adequate amount of sleep is a necessity for our health.   Lack of sleep has been associated with dementia and Alzheimer's disease.  Additionally, our mental health can be negatively affected.    Our health care workers should be monitoring how the increased screen time is affecting us.

Unfortunately, it looks like more screen time usage will be the norm for the near future.  We are not seeing a decline in COVID-19 cases.   There are school systems that began this year with in-person classes that may be going back to virtual due to the COVID-19 cases.   Some offices are continuing to keep their workers at home.   This is a very bad sign.

I think it is best to limit the amount of screen time possible.  That maybe hard when it comes to work and school.  However, for entertainment, it is possible to reduce our screen time.  People can focus on outdoor activities instead of staying inside to play video games or watch streaming shows.  People can also choose to read books instead of staring at their electronic devices.  

We are experiencing an unprecedented time in our lives right now.   We are experiencing a pandemic that is causing us to be more isolated than ever.  We need to be able to adapt to the situation while still maintaining our physical and mental health.   I think keeping our screen time as low as possible will help maintain our physical and mental health.

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?

Have you had any experience with dating? Have you ever used dating apps? If so, what has it been like for you? If not, why not?

How do you think technology — like apps, Netflix, social media and texting — affects dating and relationships? In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions? How so?

---

In my opinion, technology has definitely had an impact on the dating process, but I cannot truly say that the impact has been negative.   

In general, I think that the impact has been positive because it has made dating more accessible to people who might not have had the opportunity to date in the past.  In the past, meeting someone and starting to date them was mostly just a question of luck.  One had to be in the right place, at the right time, and had to be physically attractive enough to catch the eye of a passing stranger.  While people complain about the swipe-right culture of online dating, I don't think this is any worse (or really, any different) than meeting strangers in public used to be.  But now, more people can put themselves out there, and have many more opportunities to meet others.
IAnothertbig impact that echnology has had on dating is that it has made it easier to find people who share your interests
.  In online-dating apps, you can quickly and easily read a short paragraph about someone's interests, and even search for specific interests and filter out things that you are opposed to.  In the past, you might meet an attractive stranger, start dating, and eventually realize that you have little or nothing in common.  This could lead to painful breakups in the worst case, and to wasted time in the best case.  Technology has saved us from both outcomes.  

In thc same way, tehnology has also made it easier to find people who share your values.
  People can reveal what they think is important right away, with a carefully written introduction.  It would be difficult to reveal these things to a stranger, or even to a blind date that a friend had tried to connect you with.  

While I think that online-dating has had the biggest impact, I can't ignore the impact that social media has had on the romantic scene.  However, I have to admit, that the impact it has had is not much different than that of online-dating.  One big advantage that social media has is that it helps us to discover people who are in our close network, but who we have simply not connected with yet.  This could be colleagues at work, or friends of friends at school.  There are many connections that might have slipped away in the offline world that can easily be made online.  

As for some other suggested topics such as texting and Netflix, I think that these are worthy of note, but not really game changers in their own right.  Texting is certainly an easier way to communicate than speaking over the phone, so maybe it helps potential romantic relationships to blossom.  It is another way to get an idea of someone's interests and values before you start dating them seriously.

I was also specifically asked about Netflix, and I think that it is also noteworthy, but not game-changing.  The infamous "Netflix and Chill" date that people talk about is certainly a relic of a new tech-focused world, but is really not much more than a date that ends in "coffee" at one's apartment.  It was just a polite way to invite someone over for what you assume will be an intimate encounter.  Netflix has merely provided an opening that some people may mutually exploit.

In conclusion, I think that the future of dating will continue to be technology-focused, and I think that this is ultimately a good thing.  It will benefit a lot of people, and the one's who think that it is excessive, are probably the ones who had no trouble finding dates in the offline world.

A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out. She’s unaware that she’s actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who’s fallen for her, and is certain he’s going to get it right this time.

One day, she finds out the truth.  It was quite disconcerting.  She was sitting on her living room sofa with her boyfriend, Ted watching a movie and eating popcorn.  Ted was holding the bowl.  She turned to say something to him, and instead of the blonde haired, blue eyed, light complected man of average height she was dating, there sat a tall, dark haired man with a closely cropped beard.  He was wearing the same clothes as Ted.  He was holding the popcorn bowl like Ted, but he didn't look anything like Ted.

She hopped up off the sofa.  This couldn't be Ted, but at the same time it couldn't NOT be Ted.  She had been sitting next to this man the whole time.

"Sue," he said in a voice quite different than Ted's, "what's wrong?"

She pointed at him with a trembling finger.  He looked down and realization dawned across his handsome face.

"Sue," he said.  "Don't be afraid.  It's me.  I know I look different than I did a moment ago, but I'm still the same person that you've been dating for the past two months and the same person who sat down on the sofa an hour ago.  I admit, I look different, but it's still me."
She looked at him, then at the popcorn bowl, then back at him.
  "I don't understand," she said.

He took a deep breath and motioned for her to sit back down.  "I'll tell you," he said.

He went on to explain that he was born a shapeshifter, like his father had been.  As a child, it was hard for his parents to keep track of him.  He couldn't go to school, because when he was little, he didn't fully understand that not everyone had the same ability as he did.  Once he was old enough to understand, he didn't always have control over when he shifted.  By the time he was a teenager, he had good control but on rare occasions, it would happen unexpectedly, like it had tonight.  

Sue seemed shocked but given what she had just seen, she knew that Ted was telling the truth.  She'd seen it with her own eyes.  Seeing that she was accepting what he had told her, Ted went on.

"First, my real name is Kyle Wilkerson.  The reason I didn't tell you my real name is because I have loved you for many years and dated you four times before and it didn't work out.  I was Liam, Joe, Henry and Bob before we met while I was calling myself Ted.  I'm really sorry, but I wanted to be with you so badly that I kept trying."

ue was stunned.
  She had dated this man four times before?  She thought back and realized that each of those men after Liam had seemed to know her better than the one before.  Now she realized it was because each one DID know her better, as they had spent time together.  Ted looked anxious as Sue sat in thought.  Finally she told him that she was touched that he wanted to be with her so badly that he kept trying over and over again, but that for now she needed him to leave so she could think things through.  Ted, or actually Kyle, stood up.

"Also," she said, "what is your true form?"

He explained that he didn't know, because he had changed so often that he didn't really know what he looked like.

"What form do you feel most comfortable in?"

Before her eyes, he shrunk a couple of inches.  His hair stayed dark brown, but some light highlights appeared as it grew near shoulder length.  His nose got a little longer, his eyes changed to an emerald green.  He was stunning to look at.

"I am going to think about what I should do," Sue said.  "But if I see you again, I want you to be in this shape, because this shape is what you are most comfortable in."

Kyle smiled at her as he walked out the door.  She closed it behind him and leaned against it.  She had a lot to think about.
She went to bed that night and slept fitfully.
  She thought it was unlikely she'd ever find a man that wanted to be with her so badly.  A few days later she called him and they met for coffee.  He looked like the person he'd last shifted into, and she told him that she was willing to start over and see where it went.

They eventually married and had three children.  Sue now understood what Kyle's mother went through, as one of the three was a shapeshifter, too.  She had realized that might be the case so she was prepared, but little Ted was definitely more of a handful than his two non-shapeshifting siblings.  But she loved him as much as the others and never regretted marrying Kyle and having his children.
